steps.body: **Rain** fills rivers, lakes, ponds and wells, and soaks underground (groundwater). We get water from rivers, lakes, wells, handpumps, borewells and taps (piped from reservoirs). Most of Earth's water is **salty** sea water — we can't drink it directly.

steps.title: We use water for…
steps.body: Drinking, cooking, bathing, washing clothes and dishes, cleaning, watering plants and crops, for animals, in factories, and to make electricity at dams.

steps.title: Clean water
steps.body: Water may look clear but still have germs. Safe drinking water is **boiled**, **filtered** or **purified**. Store it in a clean, covered container and use a ladle, not hands, to take it out.

steps.title: Save water
steps.body:
- Turn off the tap while brushing.
- Use a bucket instead of a long shower.
- Fix leaking taps.
- Reuse water from washing vegetables for plants.
- Collect rainwater (rainwater harvesting).

steps.title: Water safety
steps.body: Never go near deep water, wells, ponds or rivers without an adult. Don't play in floodwater. Learn to swim only with a trained coach.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Keep a 'water diary' for a day: list every time your family uses water. Find two ways to save.

statements.s: Most of Earth's water is salty.
statements.why: Seas and oceans hold most of it.

statements.s: Clear water is always safe to drink.
statements.why: It may have invisible germs; boil or filter it.

statements.s: Turning off the tap while brushing saves water.
It is safe to play alone near a well.
Rainwater can be collected and stored.

quiz.q: Which is a way to make water safe to drink?
options: Leave it in the sun uncovered
Freeze it in a dirty bottle
quiz.why: Boiling water kills germs, so it becomes safe to drink. Adding sugar or leaving it uncovered does not make it safe.

quiz.q: Where does most river water come from?
quiz.why: Most river water comes from rain and from snow that melts on mountains.

options: Washing a car with a running hose
quiz.why: Fixing a leaking tap saves water, since a leak wastes many drops. A running tap, hose or long shower wastes it.

quiz.q: Can we drink sea water directly?
quiz.why: No. Sea water is too salty to drink.
Collecting rainwater to use later is called rainwater harvesting. It saves water.

scenes.text: Arjun in Ahmedabad tries to fly a kite on a still afternoon. It flops to the ground.
Next morning, a breeze blows. The kite soars!
'Where was the air yesterday?' he asks. His mother: 'Air is always there — wind is **moving** air.'
Later that month, monsoon clouds arrive and the weather changes completely.

steps.title: Air is all around us
steps.body: We can't see air, but we can **feel** it (wind on our face), **see what it does** (moving leaves, flying kites) and **hear** it (whistling wind). Air fills a balloon and takes up space. All living things need air; we breathe in **oxygen**, which is part of air.

steps.title: Weather
steps.body: **Weather** is what the sky and air are like on a day: sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, foggy, hot or cold. It can change in a day.

steps.title: Seasons in India
steps.body:
Many parts of India have:

- **Summer** (about March–June): hot — cotton clothes, water, caps.
- **Monsoon / rainy** (about June–September): raincoats, umbrellas.
- **Winter** (about November–February): cooler, especially in the north — woollens.

Seasons differ by place: hill areas are cool even in summer; some southern coasts stay warm all year.

steps.title: Clean air and safety
steps.body: Smoke from burning rubbish, vehicles and factories makes air dirty and can make breathing hard. Stay indoors when air is very polluted, and don't burn plastic. In a thunderstorm, stay indoors and away from tall trees.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a weather chart for a week: draw ☀️ ☁️ 🌧️ 🌬️ each day.

activity.prompt: Match the weather to what you need.

quiz.why: Wind is air that is moving. We can feel it and see it move leaves.

quiz.q: Which gas in air do we need to breathe?
quiz.why: We breathe in oxygen from the air. Smoke, dust and steam are not what we need to breathe.

quiz.q: In which season do we use umbrellas most?
quiz.why: We use umbrellas most in the monsoon, the rainy season, to keep dry.
Burning rubbish makes smoke, which makes the air dirty. Walking, cycling and planting trees keep the air clean.
During a thunderstorm, stay indoors, which is the safest place. Standing under a tall tree, swimming or flying a kite is dangerous.

scenes.text: Every morning, Fatima walks to school in Hyderabad with her elder brother Imran.
At the signal, a boy runs across while the light is red. A scooter brakes hard!
Imran holds Fatima's hand: 'Stop, look right, look left, look right again. Cross at the zebra crossing when the walking signal is green.'
At school they wash hands with soap before lunch. 'Germs are tiny, but soap beats them!'

steps.title: Hygiene habits
steps.body:
- Wash hands with **soap and water for about 20 seconds** before eating, after the toilet and after playing.
- Brush teeth twice a day.
- Bathe daily, cut nails, wear clean clothes.
- Cover your mouth and nose with your elbow or a tissue when you cough or sneeze.
- Use a toilet and keep it clean.

steps.title: Road safety
steps.body:
- Walk on the **footpath**; if none, walk facing traffic at the edge.
- Cross at a **zebra crossing** or with a traffic police signal.
- **Stop, look right, look left, look right again** before crossing (India drives on the left).
- Red = stop, yellow/amber = get ready, green = go (walking signal for people).
- Wear a helmet on a bicycle; wear a seat belt in a car.

steps.title: Safety at home
steps.body: Don't touch electric sockets, switches with wet hands, gas stoves, matches, knives or medicines. Keep away from balcony edges. If you smell gas or see fire, move out and tell an adult; call **112**.

steps.title: Strangers
steps.body: Don't go anywhere with a stranger or take sweets from them, even if they say a parent sent them. Have a family **code word**. Shout, run to a safe adult, and tell.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Sing 'Happy Birthday' twice while washing your hands — that's about 20 seconds.

activity.prompt: Put the steps for crossing a road safely in order.
items: Stop at the edge of the footpath
Look right, look left, look right again
Wait for the walking signal to turn green

quiz.q: How long should you wash hands with soap?
quiz.why: Wash your hands with soap for about 20 seconds. This is long enough to remove germs.

quiz.q: Where should we cross a road?
quiz.why: We should cross a road at a zebra crossing, which is made for people who walk. Crossing on a bend or between parked cars is unsafe.
A red traffic light means stop. Green means go.

options: Cover with your elbow or a tissue
Hold your breath for a minute
quiz.why: When you sneeze, cover your nose and mouth with your elbow or a tissue, so germs do not spread to others.

quiz.q: A stranger says 'Your mum sent me, come with me'. You…
options: Say no, run to a safe adult and tell
quiz.why: Never go with a stranger, even if they say your mum sent them. Say no, go to a safe adult and tell them.

questions.why: Rice gives us energy, because it is a carbohydrate food. Salt and water do not give energy.

questions.q: We should drink water that is…
questions.why: We should drink clean, safe water that has been boiled or filtered. Dirty or puddle water has germs, and sea water is salty.
A green walking signal means it is safe to cross, but we should still cross carefully. Red means stop.
A bucket bath uses less water than a running tap, a long shower or a leaking pipe.

questions.q: We can tell air is there because…
questions.why: We cannot see air, but we know it is there because leaves move in the wind. We see what it does.
Paneer is rich in protein, so it is a body-building food.
Before crossing, look right, left and right again, to be sure no vehicle is coming. In India traffic keeps to the left.

questions.q: Which season usually comes after summer in most of India?
questions.why: In most of India the monsoon comes after summer, around June, and brings rain.

questions.q: Why should drinking water be covered?
options: To keep dust, flies and germs out
questions.why: We should cover drinking water to keep dust, flies and germs out so it stays clean.

options: Roti, dal, sabzi and a fruit
questions.why: Roti, dal, sabzi and a fruit give energy, protein and protective food, so it is a balanced tiffin. Biscuits or chips alone are not.

questions.q: You see smoke and smell burning in your kitchen. First you should…
options: Get out and tell an adult / call 112
questions.why: If there is smoke and a burning smell, get out and tell an adult, or call 112. Never hide or pour oil on a fire.

questions.q: Why can't we see air but know it takes up space?
options: Because a balloon gets bigger when we blow air into it
Because air is heavy as stone
questions.why: When we blow air into a balloon it gets bigger, so air takes up space even though we can't see it.

courses.title: Class 3 EVS: How plants and animals live, my body, my country
courses.summary: Explore how each part of a plant works, how animals find homes, food and raise young, how to keep teeth and bones healthy, and how to read a simple map of India with directions.
outcomes: Learners can explain the job of roots, stem, leaves, flowers and seeds, and how seeds spread
Learners can describe animal homes, food habits and how some animals care for young
Learners can explain how to care for teeth, bones and muscles
Learners can use the four main directions and read a simple map with a key
Learners can name India's capital, some states and national symbols

lessons.title: How plants work and how seeds travel

scenes.text: In a park in Pune, Ira blows on a dandelion-like puffball and its fluffy seeds float away.
Her friend Hiro, whose family moved from Japan, finds winged seeds spinning down from a tree like tiny helicopters.
Ira's grandmother says, 'And mango seeds? People and animals carry those after eating the fruit!'
'Seeds travel so new plants can grow in new places,' they learn.

steps.title: Each part has a job
steps.body:
- **Roots** anchor the plant and absorb water and minerals. Some store food: **carrot, radish, beetroot**.
- **Stem** carries water up and food down; some store food: **potato** (an underground stem), **sugarcane**.
- **Leaves** make food by **photosynthesis**: using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from air. They release oxygen. Tiny holes (**stomata**) let gases in and out.
- **Flowers** make seeds. Bees and butterflies help by carrying **pollen**.
- **Seeds** have a baby plant and stored food inside.

steps.title: How seeds spread (dispersal)
steps.body:
- **Wind**: light or winged seeds (cotton, madar/aak, drumstick).
- **Water**: seeds that float (coconut).
- **Animals**: sticky or hooked seeds cling to fur; birds eat fruits and drop seeds elsewhere.
- **Bursting**: pods that pop open (peas, balsam).

Spreading out means young plants don't compete with the parent for light and water.

steps.title: Plants adapt to where they live
steps.body:
- **Cactus** (desert): thick stem stores water, spines instead of leaves to lose less water.
- **Lotus** (water): broad floating leaves with a waxy coat.
- **Pine** (cold hills): needle-shaped leaves, cone shape so snow slides off.

steps.title: Common mistake: 'plants eat soil'
steps.body: Plants take water and minerals from soil, but they **make their own food** in the leaves using sunlight. That's why a plant in a dark cupboard grows weak even with good soil.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Put a white flower or celery stalk in coloured water. After a day, see the colour reach the petals — proof the stem carries water.

activity.prompt: Match the plant part or seed to what it does.

quiz.q: What do leaves need to make food?
quiz.why: Leaves make food using sunlight, water and carbon dioxide. This is called photosynthesis.
A potato is an underground stem. The 'eyes' on a potato are buds that can grow into new plants.

quiz.q: How is a coconut seed spread?
quiz.why: A coconut has a light, fibrous husk that floats, so the sea water carries it far away to new shores. It does not use wind, hooks or bursting to spread.

quiz.q: Why does a cactus have spines?
quiz.why: A cactus lives in dry places. Its spines are tiny leaves that lose very little water, so the plant keeps its water for a long time.

quiz.q: Who helps flowers by carrying pollen?
quiz.why: Bees and butterflies carry pollen from one flower to another when they visit for nectar. This helps the flowers make seeds and fruits.

scenes.text: On a farm near Mandya, Karthik watches a weaver bird knitting a hanging nest from grass strips.
Near his feet, ants carry food into an anthill.
His uncle shows a calf drinking milk from its mother.
That evening on TV, Karthik and his cousin Amelia (in Australia) watch sea turtles lay eggs on a beach and return to the sea.

steps.title: Animal homes
steps.body:
- **Nest**: birds (weaver birds build hanging nests; tailorbirds stitch leaves).
- **Burrow**: rabbit, rat, snake.
- **Den/cave**: lion, bear, tiger.
- **Hive**: bees.
- **Anthill**: ants; **termite mound**: termites.
- **Web**: spider.
- **Shed / stable / kennel**: domestic animals people care for.

steps.title: Teeth and beaks tell what animals eat
steps.body:
- Plant-eaters (cow, goat) have flat teeth for grinding grass; many chew the cud.
- Meat-eaters (tiger) have sharp pointed teeth to tear flesh.
- Beaks: parrots crack nuts with strong curved beaks, eagles tear meat with hooked beaks, kingfishers catch fish with long pointed beaks.

steps.title: Babies: eggs or born?
steps.body:
- Animals that **lay eggs**: birds, most fish, frogs, snakes, turtles, insects.
- Animals that **give birth** to babies and feed them milk: cow, dog, cat, elephant, whale, humans (these are **mammals**).

Some parents care for young for a long time (elephants, humans); some leave the eggs (most turtles).

steps.title: Living in groups
steps.body: Elephants live in herds led by an older female. Ants and bees live in large colonies where each has a job. Group living helps find food and stay safe.

steps.title: Don't disturb
steps.body: Never touch nests or eggs — parents may abandon them. Watch wild animals from a distance; don't feed monkeys or wild animals human food.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Watch ants for 10 minutes. Where do they go? What do they carry? Draw the path.

activity.prompt: Does it lay eggs or give birth to babies?

quiz.q: Which animal lives in a burrow?
quiz.why: A rabbit digs a burrow, a hole in the ground, to live in and stay safe. Cows, fish and eagles do not live in burrows.

quiz.q: Sharp, pointed teeth are found in…
quiz.why: Tigers eat meat, so they have sharp, pointed teeth to tear it. Goats, cows and rabbits eat plants and have flat teeth.

quiz.q: Which animal gives birth and feeds its baby milk?
quiz.why: A whale is a mammal, so it gives birth to its baby and feeds it milk. Sparrows, crocodiles and turtles lay eggs.
An elephant herd is led by an older female, called the matriarch, who knows the way to food and water. A tiger would be an enemy.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't we touch birds' eggs?
quiz.why: If we touch eggs or a nest, the parent birds may get scared and leave the eggs. Then the baby birds may not hatch.

scenes.text: Sneha in Jaipur, 8, wakes up with a wobbly front tooth.
'Will I have no teeth?' she worries.
Dr Kapoor, the dentist, smiles: 'This is a milk tooth. A permanent tooth is pushing it out. Look after the new one — it has to last your whole life!'
He shows her how to brush in circles for two minutes, twice a day.

steps.title: Two sets of teeth
steps.body:
Children have **20 milk teeth**. From about age 6 they fall out one by one and **permanent teeth** grow. Adults usually have **32** permanent teeth (including wisdom teeth, which may come late or not at all).

- **Incisors** (front): cut
- **Canines** (pointed): tear
- **Molars** (back): grind

steps.title: Care for teeth
steps.body:
- Brush **twice a day** for 2 minutes with fluoride toothpaste (a pea-sized amount).
- Brush gently in small circles, on every side, and brush the tongue.
- Rinse after eating.
- Eat fewer sticky sweets and sugary drinks.
- Visit a dentist regularly.

steps.title: Bones and muscles
steps.body:
Bones make a frame called the **skeleton**. It holds us up, gives shape and protects organs: the **skull** protects the brain, **ribs** protect the heart and lungs. Adults have **206 bones**; babies are born with more, which join as they grow.

**Muscles** pull on bones to make us move. **Joints** (knee, elbow, shoulder) let us bend.

steps.title: Keep bones and muscles strong
steps.body: Eat calcium-rich foods (milk, curd, paneer, ragi, green leafy vegetables), get some sunlight (helps the body make vitamin D), play and exercise daily, and sit and stand straight.

steps.title: When to see a doctor
steps.body: Tell an adult if a tooth hurts, gums bleed a lot, or if after a fall you can't move a part, there's swelling or great pain. Don't try to pull a firmly fixed tooth yourself.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Feel your own bones: skull, jaw, ribs, elbows, knees. Bend each joint — which ones bend only one way?

statements.why: These are replaced by permanent teeth.

statements.s: Molars are used for grinding food.
statements.why: They are the broad back teeth.
The skull protects the brain; ribs protect the heart.

statements.s: Brushing once a week is enough.
Muscles help us move by pulling bones.
statements.why: Muscles pull, bones move at joints.

quiz.q: How many permanent teeth do adults usually have?
quiz.why: Adults usually have 32 permanent teeth, including the wisdom teeth. Children have 20 milk teeth.
Incisors are the sharp front teeth that cut food. Canines tear, and molars grind food.
Milk and ragi have a lot of calcium, which makes bones and teeth strong. Candy, cola and chips do not.
The ribs form a cage around the chest that protects the heart and lungs. The skull protects the brain.
We should brush our teeth for about two minutes, twice a day, so that our teeth get clean. Ten seconds is too short.

story.title: Finding the treasure on a map

scenes.text: Kabir and his friend Noor make a map of their colony in Bhopal for a treasure hunt.
They draw a compass: N at the top. The temple is to the north, the park to the east, the lake to the west.
Their teacher then shows a map of India: 'New Delhi, our capital, is in the north. Kanyakumari is at the southern tip.'
Noor finds her grandparents' home state, Kerala, in the south-west.

steps.title: Directions
steps.body:
The four main directions are **North, South, East, West**. The Sun **rises in the east** and **sets in the west**. If you face the rising Sun in the morning, north is on your left, south on your right, west behind you.

On most maps, **north is at the top**.

steps.title: Reading a map
steps.body:
A **map** is a drawing of a place seen from above. It has:

- a **title** (what place),
- a **key** or legend (symbols: 🌳 park, ➕ hospital, blue lines for rivers),
- a **direction arrow** (N),
- sometimes a **scale** (1 cm on the map = some distance on the ground).

steps.title: India facts
steps.body:
- Capital: **New Delhi**.
- India has **28 states and 8 union territories**.
- National flag: saffron, white and green with the blue **Ashoka Chakra** (24 spokes).
- National animal: **tiger**; national bird: **peacock**; national flower: **lotus**; national tree: **banyan**.
- National anthem: *Jana Gana Mana*, written by Rabindranath Tagore.
- The **Himalayas** are in the north; the southern peninsula has water on three sides: the Arabian Sea (west), Bay of Bengal (east), and the Indian Ocean (south).

steps.title: Common mistake: left and right vs east and west
steps.body: Left and right change when you turn around; **north, south, east, west don't**. That's why maps use directions.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open the Map Skills lab. Find your state. Which state is to its north? Draw a map of your room with a key.

activity.prompt: Fill in the blanks.
activity.text: The Sun rises in the ___. On most maps, ___ is at the top. The capital of India is ___. India's national animal is the ___.

quiz.why: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west. It looks like it moves, but the Earth is spinning.

quiz.q: What does a map key show?
quiz.why: A map key (legend) tells us what the signs and colours on the map mean. It is not a door key.

quiz.q: How many states does India have?
quiz.why: India has 28 states and 8 union territories. 29 or 36 are not the right count for states.
The peacock is India's national bird. It is a big, colourful bird with a long tail.

quiz.q: Which sea is to the west of India?
quiz.why: The Arabian Sea is to the west of India. The Bay of Bengal is to the east.

questions.why: The Sun rises in the east every morning. It sets in the west.

questions.q: Which animal lives in a hive?
questions.why: Bees live together in a hive. Rabbits live in burrows and lions in dens.

questions.q: Which part of the plant makes food?
questions.why: Leaves make food for the plant, using sunlight, water and air. Roots take in water and flowers make seeds.

questions.q: Children have how many milk teeth?
questions.why: Children have 20 milk teeth. Later they are replaced by 32 permanent teeth.
A crocodile lays eggs. Cows, dogs and cats give birth to babies.
The lotus is India's national flower. It grows in ponds and has pink or white petals.

questions.q: A carrot is a root that…
questions.why: A carrot is a root that stores food for the plant. We eat that stored food.
The skull is the hard bone of the head, and it protects the brain. Ribs protect the heart and lungs.

questions.q: A kingfisher's long pointed beak helps it…
questions.why: A kingfisher has a long, pointed beak that helps it catch fish from water. Other birds have different beaks for their food.

questions.q: Facing the rising Sun, north is on your…
questions.why: When you face the rising Sun, you face east. Then north is on your left and south is on your right.

questions.q: Why do seeds need to spread away from the parent plant?
options: To find space, light and water
questions.why: If seeds fall under the parent plant, they have little space, light and water. Spreading far away gives them room to grow.

questions.q: A potato is called a stem, not a root, because it…
questions.why: A potato is a stem because it has buds, called 'eyes', which grow into shoots. Roots do not have buds like that.

courses.title: Class 4 EVS & Science: Food chains, water cycle, digestion, machines
courses.summary: Understand who eats whom in nature, how water travels from sea to sky to land, what happens to food inside our body, and how simple machines make work easier.
outcomes: Learners can build a food chain and explain producers, consumers and decomposers
Learners can describe evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection
Learners can trace the path of food through the digestive system
Learners can identify levers, pulleys, wheels and axles, inclined planes, wedges and screws in daily life
Learners can explain why protecting every link in a food chain matters

scenes.text: On a school trip to a national park in Madhya Pradesh, guide Mr Baiga shows the class deer grazing.
'Tigers eat deer. Deer eat grass. So the tiger depends on the grass!' says Asha.
Mr Baiga lifts a rotting log: 'And fungi and worms break down dead plants and animals, returning goodness to the soil.'
'Everything is connected,' says Tom, a visiting student from Kenya. 'Like the lions and zebras at home.'

steps.title: Producers and consumers
steps.body:
- **Producers**: green plants make their own food from sunlight. Almost all food chains start with them.
- **Consumers**: animals that eat plants or other animals.
  - **Herbivores** eat plants (deer, grasshopper).
  - **Carnivores** eat animals (tiger, frog eats insects).
  - **Omnivores** eat both (bear, crow).
- **Decomposers**: fungi, bacteria and some small creatures break down dead things and waste, putting nutrients back into soil.

steps.title: A food chain
steps.body:
**Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle**

The arrow means '**is eaten by**' — it shows the direction food energy flows. In water: **tiny algae → small fish → big fish → kingfisher**.

steps.title: Food webs
steps.body: In nature, animals eat more than one thing, so chains link into a **food web**. A frog may eat grasshoppers and flies; a snake may eat frogs and rats. If one animal disappears, many others are affected.

steps.title: Why every link matters
steps.body: If frogs vanish from rice fields, insects that eat crops may increase. If vultures decline, dead animals lie around longer and diseases can spread. Protecting habitats protects the whole web.

steps.title: Common mistake: arrow direction
steps.body: Write grass **→** deer, not deer → grass. The arrow points from the eaten to the eater (the way energy moves).

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the Ecosystem lab, remove one animal and watch what happens to the others. Make a food chain from your own neighbourhood.

activity.prompt: Put this food chain in order (starting with the producer).

quiz.why: A mango tree is a producer because it makes its own food using sunlight. A mushroom, frog and lion cannot make their own food.

quiz.q: In 'grass → deer → tiger', the arrow means…
quiz.why: In a food chain, the arrow means 'is eaten by'. Grass is eaten by the deer, and the deer is eaten by the tiger. The energy moves along the arrow.

quiz.q: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead things are…
quiz.why: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead plants and animals are decomposers. They return nutrients to the soil.

quiz.q: A crow that eats grains and insects is a…
quiz.why: A crow eats both grains (plants) and insects (animals), so it is an omnivore.

quiz.q: If all frogs in a field disappeared, insects would probably…
quiz.why: Frogs eat insects. If all the frogs go, fewer insects get eaten, so the insects would probably increase.

scenes.text: After rain in Kolkata, there's a big puddle outside Rupa's school.
By afternoon, the Sun is out — and the puddle is gone!
At home, a cold glass of water gets tiny drops on the outside. 'Is it leaking?' asks her little brother.
Rupa's father explains: the puddle went up into the air, and the drops on the glass came from the air. It's the **water cycle**.

steps.title: 1. Evaporation
steps.body: The Sun heats water in seas, rivers, lakes and puddles. The water turns into an invisible gas called **water vapour** and rises into the air. Wet clothes dry the same way. Plants also release water vapour from their leaves.

steps.title: 2. Condensation
steps.body: High up, the air is cooler. Water vapour cools and turns back into **tiny water droplets** that gather to form **clouds**. The drops on a cold glass are condensation too — vapour from the air cooling on the glass.

steps.title: 3. Precipitation
steps.body: When droplets join and become too heavy, they fall as **rain** — or **snow** or **hail** when it is very cold.

steps.title: 4. Collection
steps.body: Rainwater flows into rivers, lakes and seas, or soaks into the ground as **groundwater**. Then the Sun heats it again and the cycle goes on — the same water has been cycling for millions of years!

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Steam you see from a kettle is actually tiny water droplets (condensed vapour); water vapour itself is **invisible**. And the drops on a cold glass do **not** leak through it.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open the Water Cycle lab. Then cover a bowl of warm water with cling film and put ice on top — watch 'rain' form inside.

activity.prompt: Put the stages of the water cycle in order, starting from water in the sea.

events.text: Vapour cools and condenses into clouds
Water collects in rivers, ground and sea

quiz.q: Water turning into vapour is called…
quiz.why: When water turns into vapour (a gas), it is called evaporation. The Sun's heat makes it happen.
Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. They form when water vapour cools and condenses.

quiz.q: Drops on the outside of a cold glass come from…
quiz.why: The drops on a cold glass come from water vapour in the air. The vapour touches the cold glass and turns into water, which is condensation.

quiz.q: Rain, snow and hail are forms of…
quiz.why: Rain, snow and hail are all water falling from clouds, which is called precipitation.

quiz.q: What gives energy to the water cycle?
quiz.why: The Sun's heat gives energy to the water cycle. It makes the water evaporate from seas and rivers.

lessons.title: The journey of food in my body

scenes.text: Nikhil in Mangaluru eats a crispy dosa and asks his mother, a nurse: 'Where does it go?'
She draws a long tube on paper: mouth → food pipe → stomach → small intestine → large intestine.
'It's a journey of many hours,' she says.
'And the good parts go into your blood to give you energy and help you grow.'

steps.title: Mouth and food pipe
steps.body: Digestion starts in the **mouth**. Teeth cut and grind food; **saliva** makes it wet and starts breaking down starch (chew a piece of roti for a long time — it begins to taste sweet!). The tongue pushes the food into the **food pipe** (oesophagus), which squeezes it down to the stomach.

steps.title: Stomach
steps.body: The **stomach** is a stretchy bag. Its muscles churn food and it adds **digestive juices** (including acid) that break food down further and kill many germs.

steps.title: Small and large intestine
steps.body:
- The **small intestine** is a long, coiled tube where most digestion is finished and nutrients pass into the **blood**.
- The **large intestine** absorbs water from what is left.
- Undigested waste leaves the body as **faeces** (poop) through the anus.

steps.title: Help your digestion
steps.body: Chew well, eat slowly, drink water, eat fibre (fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dal), and be active. Wash hands to avoid stomach infections.

steps.title: When to tell an adult
steps.body: Tell an adult if you have strong tummy pain, vomiting, diarrhoea for more than a day, or blood in your poop. With diarrhoea, drinking **ORS** (oral rehydration solution) helps replace lost water and salts; a doctor should check if it continues.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Chew a small piece of plain roti for a minute without swallowing. Does it start to taste sweet? That's saliva at work.

activity.prompt: Put the parts in the order food travels.

quiz.why: Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth chew the food and saliva mixes with it.

quiz.q: Which tube carries food from mouth to stomach?
quiz.why: The food pipe (oesophagus) carries food from the mouth to the stomach. The windpipe carries air.

quiz.q: Where do most nutrients enter the blood?
quiz.why: Most of the nutrients from digested food pass into the blood through the walls of the small intestine.
The large intestine mainly absorbs water from the food waste. What remains leaves the body as waste.

quiz.q: ORS is used when someone has…
quiz.why: ORS is given in diarrhoea, because it replaces the water and salts that the body loses.

scenes.text: In a village in Rajasthan, Kamla's grandfather pulls a heavy bucket of water from a well using a rope over a wheel.
'The pulley lets me pull **down** to lift **up** — much easier!'
At school, Kamla sees a ramp for wheelchair users and a seesaw in the playground.
Her science teacher, Mr Rao, says: 'Ramp, seesaw, pulley — all **simple machines**.'

steps.title: What a simple machine does
steps.body: A **simple machine** helps us do work with **less effort**, or changes the **direction** of a force. There are six classic types: **lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw**.

steps.title: Lever
steps.body: A rigid bar that turns on a point called the **fulcrum**. Examples: **seesaw**, **bottle opener**, **scissors** (two levers), **crowbar**, a spoon opening a tin lid. The longer the arm you push, the less effort needed.

steps.title: Pulley and wheel and axle
steps.body:
- **Pulley**: a wheel with a rope — well-pulleys, flagpoles, cranes. It can change pull-down into lift-up.
- **Wheel and axle**: a wheel fixed to a rod — bicycle, doorknob, tap, steering wheel.

steps.title: Inclined plane, wedge, screw
steps.body:
- **Inclined plane** (ramp): it's easier to push a heavy load up a slope than lift it straight up — ramps, slides, hill roads that zig-zag.
- **Wedge**: two slopes together that split or cut — knife, axe, nail tip.
- **Screw**: an inclined plane wrapped around a rod — screws, bottle caps, jar lids.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Use knives, scissors and tools only with adult permission. Keep fingers away from pulleys and moving wheels.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Find at least 5 simple machines in your kitchen (knife, bottle opener, tongs, jar lid, rolling pin, tap). Which type is each?

activity.prompt: Match each object with its simple machine.

quiz.why: A seesaw is a lever. It rests and turns on a point in the middle, called the fulcrum.

quiz.q: Why is a ramp easier than lifting straight up?
options: It needs less effort, over a longer distance
quiz.why: A ramp is a slope. It lets us use less effort than lifting straight up, but we move over a longer distance.
An axe is a wedge. Its thin sharp edge pushes into wood and splits it.

quiz.q: The point a lever turns on is the…
quiz.why: The fixed point on which a lever turns is called the fulcrum.

quiz.q: A screw is an inclined plane…
quiz.why: A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a rod. The slope winds around like a spiral.

questions.why: Green plants make their own food, so they are producers. Consumers eat other living things, and decomposers break down dead things.
Clouds form by condensation. Water vapour cools and turns into tiny droplets.
A bottle opener is a lever. You press down on one end and the cap lifts at the other.

questions.q: Food goes from the mouth to the…
questions.why: Food goes from the mouth down the food pipe (oesophagus) to the stomach. The lungs and heart are for other jobs.
A mushroom is a fungus and a decomposer, because it breaks down dead matter. Deer, tiger and grass are not decomposers.
Wet clothes dry because the water in them evaporates into the air. The Sun and wind help.

questions.q: Which is a correct food chain?
questions.why: A food chain starts with the producer, and the arrows point to the eater. Grass is eaten by deer, and the deer is eaten by tiger.

options: Break down food and kill many germs
questions.why: Acid in the stomach helps break food down and kills many germs that come in with the food.
A doorknob is a wheel and axle, because turning the larger knob turns the small axle inside easily.

questions.q: Hill roads zig-zag because a long gentle slope…
options: Needs less effort than a steep one
questions.why: A long, gentle slope needs less effort than a steep one, so hill roads zig-zag. It is the inclined plane idea.

questions.q: If decomposers vanished, what would happen?
options: Dead things and waste would pile up and soil would lose nutrients
questions.why: Without decomposers, dead plants, animals and waste would pile up, and the soil would not get nutrients back. Plants would not grow well.

questions.q: Why does a chewed piece of roti start to taste sweet?
questions.why: Saliva has a juice that breaks starch in roti into sugar, so a chewed piece starts to taste sweet. The roti has no honey.

courses.title: Class 5 EVS & Science: Earth, environment, health and India
courses.summary: Learn how Earth moves to make day, night and seasons, how matter changes state, how to protect the environment, how germs spread and basic first aid, and the rich diversity of India's regions.
outcomes: Learners can explain day and night, the year, and the Moon's light
Learners can classify solids, liquids and gases and describe melting, freezing, evaporation and condensation
Learners can explain pollution and practise reduce, reuse, recycle
Learners can explain how germs spread and give simple first aid for small cuts, burns and nosebleeds
Learners can locate regions of India and describe how land, climate, food and clothing vary

scenes.text: At 7 p.m. in Delhi, Tanvi video-calls her uncle Mohan in New York. He's eating breakfast!
'How is it night here and morning there?' Tanvi asks.
Her father shines a torch on a ball and spins it slowly. One side is lit; the other is dark.
Later, they look at the half Moon. 'The Moon doesn't make its own light — it reflects the Sun's,' Papa says.

steps.title: The Sun and the planets
steps.body: The **Sun** is a star — a huge ball of hot gas that gives light and heat. Eight planets go around it: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. Jupiter is the largest; Mercury is closest to the Sun. Earth is the only planet known to have life.

steps.title: Day and night: rotation
steps.body: Earth **spins** on its axis (an imaginary line through the North and South Poles) about once every **24 hours**. The side facing the Sun has **day**; the side facing away has **night**. Because Earth spins from west to east, the Sun appears to rise in the east.

steps.title: A year: revolution
steps.body: Earth also travels **around** the Sun. One trip takes about **365¼ days** — one year. The extra quarter-days add up, so every 4th year (usually) gets an extra day, 29 February — a **leap year**. Earth's axis is tilted, and that tilt (not distance from the Sun) mainly causes the **seasons**.

steps.title: The Moon
steps.body: The Moon goes around Earth in about a month (roughly 27–29½ days depending on how you measure). It reflects sunlight. As it moves, we see different amounts of its lit side — the **phases**: new moon → crescent → half → full moon → and back. **Amavasya** is the new moon and **Purnima** the full moon in the Indian calendar.

steps.title: Safety: never look at the Sun
steps.body: Never look directly at the Sun — not even during an eclipse — without proper certified solar-eclipse glasses. It can permanently damage your eyes.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Open the Solar Scale lab to compare planet sizes. Observe the Moon every few nights for two weeks and draw its shape.

statements.s: Day and night happen because Earth goes around the Sun.
statements.why: They happen because Earth spins (rotates) on its axis.

statements.s: The Moon makes its own light.

statements.why: It is the biggest in our solar system.

quiz.q: How long does Earth take to spin once?
quiz.why: The Earth spins once on its axis in about 24 hours. This makes one day and night.

quiz.q: How many planets go around the Sun?
quiz.why: There are eight planets that go around the Sun, including Earth.

quiz.q: Why is it night in India when it is morning in New York?
options: They are on opposite sides of the spinning Earth
quiz.why: The Earth spins, so only half of it faces the Sun at a time. India and New York are on opposite sides, so when it is night in one, it is day in the other.
The full moon day is called Purnima. The new moon day is Amavasya.

quiz.q: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
quiz.why: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Venus, Earth and Mars are farther away.

scenes.text: Sameer's father sells kulfi from a cart in Amritsar. On a hot afternoon, a kulfi drips into a sticky puddle.
In the evening, his father puts the milk mixture in moulds in the freezer — it becomes solid again.
Tea boils on the stove at home and steam rises.
'Same stuff, different states!' says Sameer.

steps.title: Three states of matter
steps.body:
Everything that takes up space and has weight is **matter**.

- **Solid**: fixed shape and size (stone, ice, wood).
- **Liquid**: fixed amount but takes the shape of its container; flows (water, milk, oil).
- **Gas**: no fixed shape or size; spreads to fill any space (air, steam, the smell of agarbatti spreading).

steps.title: Changing state
steps.body:
- **Melting**: solid → liquid when heated (ice → water, butter on hot roti).
- **Freezing**: liquid → solid when cooled (water → ice; pure water freezes at **0 °C**).
- **Evaporation/boiling**: liquid → gas (pure water boils at **100 °C** at sea level).
- **Condensation**: gas → liquid when cooled (mist on a mirror after a bath).

steps.title: Dissolving
steps.body: Some solids **dissolve** in water (sugar, salt) — they seem to disappear but are still there; you can taste them. Others don't (sand, chalk). Evaporating salty water leaves the salt behind — that is how salt is made in salt pans along coasts such as in Gujarat.

steps.title: Safety with heat
steps.body: Steam can burn worse than you expect. Keep away from boiling pots and pressure cookers, and let an adult handle them.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Put an ice cube in a steel plate and watch it melt. Then leave the water in the sun. Where did it go?

activity.prompt: Solid, liquid or gas?

quiz.q: Which takes the shape of its container but keeps the same amount?
quiz.why: A liquid takes the shape of its container but keeps the same amount. A solid keeps its own shape, and a gas spreads to fill the container.
When ice changes into water, it is melting, which is a change from solid to liquid.

quiz.q: At what temperature does pure water boil at sea level?
quiz.why: Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level. It freezes at 0 °C.

quiz.q: Mist on a bathroom mirror is…
quiz.why: Mist on a bathroom mirror is condensation: steam cools on the mirror and turns into tiny drops of water.
Sugar dissolves in water, and the water tastes sweet. Plastic, stone and sand do not dissolve.

scenes.text: In Indore, Class 5 student Ananya notices plastic bags blocking a drain. After heavy rain, the street floods.
Worse, she sees a cow chewing a plastic bag.
She and her friends start a 'Bring your own bag' drive with cloth bags made from old clothes.
Shopkeepers join in. The class also starts a compost pit for kitchen waste in the school garden.

steps.title: Pollution
steps.body:
**Pollution** is harmful material in air, water or land.

- **Air**: vehicle and factory smoke, burning waste and crop stubble, dust.
- **Water**: sewage, factory waste, plastic and chemicals in rivers and seas.
- **Land**: litter, plastic, too many chemicals in fields.
- **Noise**: loud horns, loudspeakers, firecrackers.

steps.title: Reduce, reuse, recycle
steps.body:
- **Reduce**: use less — carry a water bottle and cloth bag, say no to extra packaging, switch off lights and fans.
- **Reuse**: use things again — jars for storage, old clothes as cleaning cloths, both sides of paper.
- **Recycle**: send paper, metal, glass and some plastics to be made into new things.

Also **compost** kitchen waste (peels, leaves) into rich soil.

steps.title: Segregate waste
steps.body: Many Indian cities ask homes to separate waste: **wet** (food, peels — compostable) and **dry** (paper, plastic, metal, glass — recyclable). **Hazardous** items (batteries, medicines, bulbs, e-waste) need special collection.

steps.title: People who protected nature
steps.body: In the **Chipko movement** of the 1970s in the Himalayan region (now Uttarakhand), villagers — many of them women — hugged trees to stop them being cut. The Bishnoi community of Rajasthan is known for protecting trees and blackbuck for centuries.

steps.title: Don't burn waste
steps.body: Burning plastic and rubbish releases harmful smoke. Report illegal dumping to local authorities with an adult.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Do a one-day waste audit at home: list everything thrown away. Which could be reduced, reused, recycled or composted?

a.text: You're buying vegetables. The seller offers a plastic bag. You forgot your cloth bag. What do you do?

choices.label: Take three plastic bags
choices.feedback: Each bag may be used for minutes but last in the environment for a very long time.

choices.label: Put everything in your school bag or carry it in your hands
choices.feedback: Great — you reduced plastic!

choices.label: Take one bag and reuse it many times
choices.feedback: Good — reuse is the next-best choice.

b.text: On the way home, you see a cow eating a plastic bag from a pile. How do you feel, and what will you do next time?

choices.label: Keep a cloth bag in my school bag always
choices.feedback: Planning ahead is the best fix.

c.text: At home there are banana peels and a broken plastic toy. Where do they go?

choices.label: Peels in wet waste/compost, toy in dry waste
choices.feedback: Correct segregation!

choices.label: Both in one bin
choices.feedback: Mixed waste is hard to recycle or compost.

e.text: Try separating: wet waste rots and can become compost; dry waste can be recycled.

choices.label: Separate them
choices.feedback: Well done.

d.text: You reduced plastic and segregated waste. Small daily choices, multiplied by millions of people, protect the planet!

options: Using a glass jar to store pencils
quiz.why: Using a glass jar again to store pencils is reuse. Throwing it away or burning paper is not.
Banana peels are wet waste, which rots naturally, so it can be made into compost.
The Chipko movement was about saving trees. Villagers hugged the trees so that no one could cut them.
Burning rubbish makes smoke, which pollutes the air. Cycling, composting and planting trees do not.
Old batteries have harmful chemicals, so they must go to special hazardous or e-waste collection, not in the garden or river.

scenes.text: Ravi in Patna falls while skating and scrapes his knee. It's bleeding a little.
His friend Aisha stays calm: 'Let's tell your mum.'
Ravi's mother washes the scrape gently under clean running water, presses a clean cloth on it, and puts on a bandage.
'Cleaning stops germs getting in,' she says. 'Germs are too small to see, but they can make wounds infected.'

steps.title: What germs are
steps.body: **Germs** (microbes) are tiny living things — bacteria, viruses and others — too small to see without a microscope. Many are harmless or even helpful (bacteria that turn milk into curd). Some cause illness: colds, flu, diarrhoea, typhoid, malaria (spread by mosquitoes).

steps.title: How germs spread
steps.body:
- Through the **air** when people cough or sneeze (cold, flu, tuberculosis).
- Through **dirty water and food** (diarrhoea, typhoid, cholera).
- Through **insects** like mosquitoes (malaria, dengue) and flies.
- Through **touch** — dirty hands to mouth, eyes, nose.

steps.title: Staying healthy
steps.body: Wash hands with soap; drink safe water; cover food; don't let water collect in pots, coolers or tyres (mosquitoes breed in still water); sleep under a net or use repellent where mosquitoes are common; get **vaccines** as advised by doctors — they train the body to fight specific germs.

steps.title: Simple first aid
steps.body:
- **Small cut or scrape**: wash with clean running water, press with a clean cloth to stop bleeding, cover with a bandage.
- **Minor burn**: cool under cool running water for about 20 minutes; don't put ice, toothpaste or butter on it; cover loosely with a clean cloth.
- **Nosebleed**: sit up, lean **forward** (not back), pinch the soft part of the nose for 10 minutes.
- Always tell an adult.

steps.title: When it's an emergency
steps.body: Call an adult and **112** if someone is not breathing, is unconscious, bleeding heavily, badly burnt, or had a serious fall or bite. First aid is help until a doctor or ambulance arrives — this is general education, not medical advice.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With an adult, look inside your family's first-aid box. Is there soap, clean bandages, antiseptic, gauze and a list of emergency numbers?

activity.prompt: Questions kids often ask about germs and getting hurt

items.q: If I can't see germs, how do I know they're there?
items.a: Scientists see them with microscopes. That's why we wash hands even when they look clean.

items.q: Should I put toothpaste on a burn?
items.a: No. Cool it under cool running water for about 20 minutes and tell an adult.

items.q: Why lean forward for a nosebleed?
items.a: Leaning back makes blood run down your throat, which can make you feel sick. Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.
A quick pinch for a moment. They protect you from serious diseases for a long time.
No. Many are harmless and some are helpful, like the bacteria that make curd or live in our gut.

quiz.why: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes. A mosquito bite passes the germ into the blood.

quiz.q: For a minor burn you should…
options: Cool under running water for about 20 minutes
quiz.why: For a small burn, cool the place under running water for about 20 minutes. Do not put ice, butter or toothpaste.
During a nosebleed, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose. Leaning back lets blood go down the throat.

quiz.q: Which helpful thing do bacteria do?
quiz.why: Some bacteria are helpful. For example, they turn milk into curd. Others cause diseases.

quiz.q: Why empty water from old tyres and coolers?
quiz.why: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, so we should empty water from old tyres and coolers to stop mosquitoes breeding.

lessons.title: Unity in diversity: regions of India

scenes.text: During the summer break, the Mehta family from Gujarat travels by train across India.
In Himachal Pradesh, people wear woollens and live in houses with sloping roofs. In Rajasthan, they cross sand dunes and see camels.
In Kerala, they eat appam with stew and see backwaters and coconut trees. In Assam, they visit tea gardens.
'So many languages, foods and clothes — and we're all Indian!' says young Jhanvi.

steps.title: Physical regions
steps.body:
- **Himalayan mountains** in the north: snow, rivers like the Ganga and Brahmaputra begin in or flow from this region.
- **Northern plains**: flat, fertile land along big rivers — lots of farming.
- **Thar Desert** in the west (mostly Rajasthan): very little rain, hot days, cold nights.
- **Deccan Plateau** in the south-centre: raised, rocky land.
- **Coastal plains** along the east and west coasts.
- **Islands**: Andaman & Nicobar (Bay of Bengal) and Lakshadweep (Arabian Sea).

steps.title: Land shapes life
steps.body: Where people live affects their food, clothes and houses. Coastal areas eat a lot of fish and coconut; the plains grow wheat and rice; the desert uses millet like bajra; cold hills need thick clothes and warm homes. Rain-heavy Meghalaya and dry western Rajasthan are very different.

steps.title: Many languages
steps.body: India's Constitution lists **22 scheduled languages** in its Eighth Schedule, including Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Punjabi, Assamese, Urdu and Sanskrit, and hundreds more languages and dialects are spoken. Hindi in Devanagari script is the official language of the Union, with English also used officially.

steps.title: Festivals and harvests
steps.body: Many harvest festivals fall in mid-January: **Pongal** (Tamil Nadu), **Makar Sankranti** and **Uttarayan** (many states), **Lohri** (Punjab, the night before), **Magh/Bhogali Bihu** (Assam). Different names, the same thanks for the harvest.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: In the Map Skills lab, find the Himalayas, the Thar Desert and the Deccan Plateau. Ask a classmate from another state about their food and festivals.

activity.prompt: Match the region with a feature.
pairs: Raised, rocky land in the south-centre

quiz.q: Where is the Thar Desert mostly?
quiz.why: The Thar Desert is mostly in western Rajasthan. It is hot and dry.

quiz.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule?
quiz.why: The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists 22 languages of India.

quiz.q: Which festival is a harvest festival of Tamil Nadu?
quiz.why: Pongal is the harvest festival of Tamil Nadu. Onam is Kerala's festival, Bihu is Assam's and Lohri is Punjab's.

quiz.q: Andaman & Nicobar Islands are in the…
quiz.why: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal, east of the Indian mainland.

quiz.q: Why do houses in snowy hills have sloping roofs?
options: So snow and rain slide off
quiz.why: Houses in snowy hills have sloping roofs so that snow and rain slide off and do not pile up.

questions.q: Earth spinning on its axis causes…
questions.why: The Earth spinning on its axis causes day and night. The seasons come from its path around the Sun.
Water freezing into ice is a change from liquid to solid.

questions.q: Which is a way to reduce waste?
questions.why: Carrying a cloth bag cuts down waste, because we do not need plastic bags. Littering and burning rubbish are harmful.

questions.q: Which planet do we live on?
questions.why: We live on the planet Earth.

questions.q: Germs in dirty water can cause…
questions.why: Germs in dirty water can make us ill with diarrhoea. They do not cause broken bones or sunburn.

questions.q: Which state is famous for tea gardens and Bihu?
questions.why: Assam is famous for its tea gardens and the Bihu festival.

questions.q: About how many days does Earth take to go around the Sun?
questions.why: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to go around the Sun, which is one year.

questions.q: Salt is obtained from sea water by…
questions.why: Salt is taken from sea water by evaporation. The sun dries the water and the salt is left behind.

questions.q: For a nosebleed, the right first aid is…
options: Lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
questions.why: For a nosebleed, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose. Tilting the head back or lying down is wrong.

options: Earth's distance from the Sun only
Earth's tilted axis as it goes around the Sun
questions.why: The Earth's axis is tilted as it goes around the Sun, so different parts get more or less direct sunlight at different times. This causes the seasons.

questions.q: Why should we separate wet and dry waste?
options: So wet waste can be composted and dry waste recycled
questions.why: If we keep wet and dry waste apart, wet waste can be made into compost and dry waste can be recycled.

questions.q: Why do we see phases of the Moon?
options: We see different parts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth
questions.why: The Moon goes around the Earth, and we see different parts of its sunlit half. This gives the phases. Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not phases.

school-primary-hindi.title: Pathshala Primary Hindi (हिंदी, Class 1–5)
school-primary-hindi.description: Hindi basics for young learners: varnamala, matras, words, sentences, grammar and original poems — with English help for new learners.

courses.title: हिंदी कक्षा 1: वर्णमाला और पहले शब्द (Varnamala & first words)
courses.summary: Meet the Hindi alphabet — स्वर (vowels) and व्यंजन (consonants) — read simple words without matras, and enjoy a first original poem. English help is given for new learners.
outcomes: Learners can say and recognise the 11 स्वर and अं, अः
Learners can say and recognise the व्यंजन from क to ह and the joined letters क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ, श्र
Learners can read and write two- and three-letter words without matras (घर, जल, कमल)
Learners can recite a short poem and find rhyming words

scenes.text: दिल्ली में छह साल की पिहू हिंदी सीख रही है। उसकी दोस्त एमा (Emma) जर्मनी से आई है और वह भी सीखना चाहती है।
दीदी कहती हैं: 'अ से अनार, आ से आम!'
पिहू जोड़ती है: 'इ से इमली, ई से ईख, उ से उल्लू!'
एमा हँसती है: 'Every vowel has a picture-word. Now I can remember!'

steps.title: स्वर क्या हैं? (What are swar?)
steps.body:
**स्वर** वे अक्षर हैं जिन्हें हम बिना किसी दूसरे अक्षर की मदद के बोल सकते हैं।

हिंदी में 11 स्वर हैं: **अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ए ऐ ओ औ**

इनके साथ **अं** (anusvar) और **अः** (visarga) भी पढ़े जाते हैं।

*Swar are vowels — sounds you can say on their own.*
steps.say: स्वर: अ आ इ ई उ ऊ ऋ ए ऐ ओ औ

steps.title: चित्र-शब्द (Picture words)
steps.body:
- **अ** — अनार (pomegranate)
- **आ** — आम (mango)
- **इ** — इमली (tamarind)
- **ई** — ईख (sugarcane)
- **उ** — उल्लू (owl)
- **ऊ** — ऊन (wool)
- **ऋ** — ऋषि (sage)
- **ए** — एड़ी (heel)
- **ऐ** — ऐनक (spectacles)
- **ओ** — ओखली (mortar)
- **औ** — औरत (woman)
- **अं** — अंगूर (grapes)

steps.title: छोटा और बड़ा (short and long)
steps.body:
कुछ स्वर जोड़ी में आते हैं — एक छोटा, एक लंबा:

- **अ** (short a) — **आ** (long aa)
- **इ** (short i) — **ई** (long ee)
- **उ** (short u) — **ऊ** (long oo)

लंबे स्वर को थोड़ा खींचकर बोलें। *Say the long vowel a little longer.*

steps.title: आम गलती (Common mistake)
steps.body: **इ** और **ई** एक जैसे दिखते हैं। ई के ऊपर एक घुमावदार रेखा होती है। **उ** और **ऊ** में भी ध्यान दें — ऊ के नीचे एक और मोड़ होता है।

steps.title: करके देखो (Try this)
steps.body: घर में ऐसी चीज़ें ढूँढो जिनका नाम किसी स्वर से शुरू हो: आम, अलमारी, इत्र, ऊन…

quiz.q: हिंदी में कितने स्वर हैं? (How many swar?)
quiz.why: हिंदी में 11 स्वर हैं: अ, आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ, ए, ऐ, ओ, औ। 33 व्यंजन अलग होते हैं।

quiz.q: 'आम' किस स्वर से शुरू होता है?
quiz.why: 'आम' शब्द 'आ' स्वर से शुरू होता है। आम का पहला अक्षर 'आ' है।
'उल्लू' शब्द का पहला अक्षर 'उ' है, छोटा उ। ऊ बड़ा ऊ होता है।

quiz.q: Which is the long form of इ?
quiz.why: इ का बड़ा रूप ई है। इ छोटी इ है और ई बड़ी ई, उसकी मात्रा 'ी' होती है।
'अंगूर' शब्द 'अं' से शुरू होता है, जिसमें अ के ऊपर बिंदु है।

scenes.text: लखनऊ में आरव की दादी ने उसे व्यंजन सिखाने के लिए एक खेल बनाया।
हर कार्ड पर एक अक्षर और एक चित्र: क से कबूतर, ख से खरगोश, ग से गमला।
दादी कहती हैं: 'देखो, हर पंक्ति मुँह के एक हिस्से से बोली जाती है — क-ख-ग-घ गले से!'
एक हफ्ते में आरव ने सारे व्यंजन पहचान लिए।

steps.title: व्यंजन (Consonants)
steps.body:
**व्यंजन** को बोलने में स्वर की मदद लगती है — हर व्यंजन में छिपा हुआ **अ** होता है: क = क् + अ।

पाँच-पाँच के वर्ग (groups):

- **क ख ग घ ङ**
- **च छ ज झ ञ**
- **ट ठ ड ढ ण**
- **त थ द ध न**
- **प फ ब भ म**

और: **य र ल व**, **श ष स ह**

steps.title: चित्र-शब्द
steps.body: क — कबूतर · ख — खरगोश · ग — गमला · घ — घड़ी · च — चम्मच · छ — छतरी · ज — जहाज़ · झ — झंडा · ट — टमाटर · ठ — ठठेरा · ड — डमरू · ढ — ढोल · त — तितली · थ — थर्मस · द — दवात · ध — धनुष · न — नल · प — पतंग · फ — फल · ब — बत्तख · भ — भालू · म — मछली · य — यज्ञ · र — रथ · ल — लड्डू · व — वन · श — शलगम · ष — षट्कोण · स — सेब · ह — हाथी

steps.title: संयुक्त व्यंजन (Joined letters)
steps.body:
दो व्यंजन मिलकर नया अक्षर बनाते हैं:

- **क्ष** = क् + ष (क्षत्रिय, कक्षा)
- **त्र** = त् + र (त्रिशूल, पत्र)
- **ज्ञ** = ज् + ञ (ज्ञान)
- **श्र** = श् + र (श्रमिक)

steps.title: कहाँ से बोलें (Where the sound comes from)
steps.body: क-वर्ग गले से, च-वर्ग तालु (roof of mouth) से, ट-वर्ग जीभ मोड़कर, त-वर्ग दाँतों से, प-वर्ग होंठों से। हर वर्ग का दूसरा और चौथा अक्षर साँस के झोंके (breath) के साथ बोलें: क-**ख**, ग-**घ**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: **ब** और **व** मिलते-जुलते हैं — ब के बीच में एक तिरछी रेखा होती है। **घ** और **ध**, **म** और **भ** को भी ध्यान से देखें।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने परिवार के सदस्यों के नाम का पहला व्यंजन लिखो: मम्मी — म, पापा — प, दीदी — द।

activity.prompt: अक्षर को सही चित्र-शब्द से मिलाओ (Match the letter to its word).

quiz.q: 'हाथी' किस व्यंजन से शुरू होता है?
quiz.why: 'हाथी' शब्द में पहला व्यंजन 'ह' है। ह से हाथी बनता है।

quiz.q: क्ष किन दो अक्षरों से बना है?
quiz.why: संयुक्त अक्षर 'क्ष' दो अक्षरों से बना है: क् और ष। क् + ष = क्ष।

quiz.q: Which group is said with the lips?
quiz.why: प, फ, ब, भ, म होंठों से बोले जाते हैं। इसलिए इस समूह को प-वर्ग कहते हैं।
'मछली' का पहला अक्षर 'म' है। मछली म से शुरू होती है।
'ज्ञान' शब्द में संयुक्त अक्षर 'ज्ञ' है। झंडा, जल और जहाज़ में ज्ञ नहीं है।

lessons.title: बिना मात्रा के शब्द (Words without matras)

scenes.text: पटना में रिया अपने घर की चीज़ों पर पर्चियाँ चिपका रही है।
दरवाज़े के पास लिखा: **घर**। पानी के मटके पर: **जल**। फूलदान पर: **कमल**।
पापा हैरान: 'तुमने बिना किसी मात्रा के इतने शब्द लिख दिए!'
रिया: 'हर अक्षर में अ छिपा है, इसलिए ये शब्द आसानी से बन जाते हैं!'

steps.title: दो अक्षर के शब्द
steps.body:
जब हम दो व्यंजन साथ रखते हैं तो शब्द बनता है:

- **घ + र = घर** (house)
- **ज + ल = जल** (water)
- **फ + ल = फल** (fruit)
- **न + ल = नल** (tap)
- **ब + स = बस** (bus / enough)
- **क + ल = कल** (yesterday / tomorrow)

steps.title: तीन और चार अक्षर के शब्द
steps.body:
- **कमल** (lotus) = क + म + ल
- **नमक** (salt) = न + म + क
- **शहर** (city) = श + ह + र
- **बतख** (duck) = ब + त + ख
- **सड़क** (road) = स + ड़ + क
- **अजगर** (python) = अ + ज + ग + र

steps.title: छोटे वाक्य
steps.body:
- **कमल जल पर है।** (The lotus is on the water — 'पर' and 'है' are useful helper words.)
- **नल चल रहा है।**
- **बस रुक गई।**

(Some helper words like है and गई have matras — you'll learn those next!)

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: शब्द के अक्षरों के बीच जगह मत छोड़ो: **क मल** ❌ → **कमल** ✅। पर दो शब्दों के बीच जगह ज़रूरी है: **कमलजल** ❌ → **कमल जल** ✅। शिरोरेखा (the top line) पूरे शब्द पर एक साथ खींचो।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: इन अक्षरों से कितने शब्द बना सकते हो? **म, न, क, ल, र, घ** — जैसे: मन, कल, घर, नमक, कमल।

activity.prompt: अक्षर जोड़कर शब्द लिखो (Join the letters to write the word).

quiz.why: 'जल' का मतलब पानी है, यानी English में water।
क, म और ल को क्रम से मिलाने पर 'कमल' बनता है। कमल एक फूल है, lotus।
'फल' का मतलब fruit है। बस, नल और घर के अर्थ दूसरे हैं।
सही लिखावट 'कमल' है, जिसमें अक्षर बिना जगह छोड़े साथ-साथ लिखे जाते हैं।
'नमक' में तीन अक्षर हैं: न, म और क। गिनकर देखो।

scenes.text: जयपुर में स्कूल की प्रार्थना-सभा के बाद टीचर मीनू जी एक नई कविता सिखाती हैं।
बच्चे ताली बजाकर गाते हैं: 'सूरज दादा आए हैं…'
छोटा कबीर खिड़की से बाहर चिड़िया देखता है — 'वह भी गा रही है!'
सब बच्चे कविता घर जाकर अपने परिवार को सुनाते हैं।

steps.title: कविता: सूरज दादा (VidyaVerse original)
steps.body:
**सूरज दादा आए हैं,**
**किरणें सुनहरी लाए हैं।**
**चिड़िया चूँ-चूँ गाती है,**
**सबको रोज़ जगाती है।**

**फूल खिले हैं बगिया में,**
**ओस चमकती पत्तियों में।**
**उठो-उठो, अब आँखें खोलो,**
**सबसे मीठी बोली बोलो।**
steps.say: सूरज दादा आए हैं, किरणें सुनहरी लाए हैं। चिड़िया चूँ-चूँ गाती है, सबको रोज़ जगाती है।

steps.title: शब्दों के अर्थ (Word meanings)
steps.body:
- **किरणें** — rays
- **सुनहरी** — golden
- **बगिया** — little garden
- **ओस** — dew
- **बोली** — way of speaking / words

steps.title: तुक वाले शब्द (Rhyming words)
steps.body: कविता में आख़िरी शब्द मिलते-जुलते हैं: **आए — लाए**, **गाती — जगाती**, **खोलो — बोलो**। इन्हें **तुकांत शब्द** कहते हैं।

steps.title: कविता कैसे सुनाएँ
steps.body: धीरे और साफ़ बोलो, हर पंक्ति के बाद थोड़ा रुको, और चेहरे पर मुस्कान रखो। हाथों से इशारे करो: सूरज के लिए हाथ ऊपर, चिड़िया के लिए पंख।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'पानी' और 'रानी' की तरह तीन और तुकांत जोड़ियाँ बनाओ: नाना — गाना, मोर — शोर…

activity.prompt: तुकांत शब्द मिलाओ (Match the rhyming words).

quiz.q: कविता में सूरज को क्या कहा गया है?
quiz.why: कविता में सूरज को 'सूरज दादा' कहा गया है, जैसे वे घर आए हों। यह कविता की पंक्ति से पता चलता है।
'किरणें' का अर्थ rays है, यानी सूरज की रोशनी की धाराएँ।
'गाती' का तुकांत शब्द 'जगाती' है, क्योंकि दोनों के अंत में 'ती' आता है।
चिड़िया 'चूँ-चूँ' करके गाती है। कौआ काँव-काँव करता है।
'ओस' का अर्थ dew है, यानी सुबह पत्तों पर पानी की छोटी बूँदें।

questions.q: 'आ' से कौन-सा फल शुरू होता है?
questions.why: 'आ' से आम फल शुरू होता है। सेब 'से', अंगूर 'अं' और केला 'के' से शुरू होता है।
'इ' एक स्वर है। त, क और म व्यंजन हैं।
'घर' का अर्थ house है, यानी रहने की जगह।

questions.q: 'तितली' किस अक्षर से शुरू होता है?
questions.why: 'तितली' शब्द 'त' अक्षर से शुरू होता है। द, ट और थ दूसरे अक्षर हैं।
ऊ बड़ा (दीर्घ) स्वर है। उ, अ और इ छोटे (ह्रस्व) स्वर हैं।
न और ल मिलकर 'नल' बनता है। नल से पानी आता है।

questions.q: त्र किन अक्षरों से बना है?
questions.why: 'त्र' अक्षर त् और र से बना है, जैसे पत्र और मित्र में।
'कमल' का अर्थ lotus है, एक सुंदर फूल जो तालाब में खिलता है।

questions.q: क-वर्ग के अक्षर कहाँ से बोले जाते हैं?
questions.why: क वर्ग के अक्षर (क, ख, ग, घ, ङ) गले (कंठ) से बोले जाते हैं।
'खोलो' का उलटा (तुकांत यहाँ) 'बोलो' है, क्योंकि दोनों के अंत में 'ओलो' आता है।

questions.q: हिंदी के हर व्यंजन में कौन-सा स्वर छिपा होता है?
questions.why: हर व्यंजन में 'अ' स्वर छिपा होता है। जैसे क = क् + अ।

questions.q: Which word has 4 letters and no matras?
questions.why: 'अजगर' में चार अक्षर हैं (अ-ज-ग-र) और कोई मात्रा नहीं है। घर में दो अक्षर हैं, कमल में तीन, आम में आ की मात्रा है।

courses.title: हिंदी कक्षा 2–3: मात्राएँ, शब्द और वाक्य (Matras, words & sentences)
courses.summary: Learn every matra (vowel sign) — ा ि ी ु ू ृ े ै ो ौ ं ँ — read and write words with them, and build simple sentences about daily life.
outcomes: Learners can name each matra and the स्वर it stands for
Learners can read and write words using आ, इ, ई, उ, ऊ, ऋ matras
Learners can read and write words using ए, ऐ, ओ, औ, अं and चंद्रबिंदु
Learners can write simple sentences with है / हैं and ending marks

lessons.title: आ, इ, ई की मात्राएँ (aa, i, ee signs)

scenes.text: भोपाल में मीरा की दीदी कॉलेज में पढ़ती हैं। मीरा उनकी डायरी में लिखा पढ़ने की कोशिश करती है: **दीदी**।
'द के आगे यह लंबी लकीर क्या है?' मीरा पूछती है।
दीदी बताती हैं: 'यह **ई की मात्रा** है। स्वर जब व्यंजन से मिलता है, तो **मात्रा** बनकर आता है।'
मीरा तुरंत पढ़ती है: दादा, दिन, दीया!

steps.title: मात्रा क्या है? (What is a matra?)
steps.body:
जब कोई स्वर व्यंजन के साथ जुड़ता है, तो वह एक छोटे चिह्न (sign) के रूप में लिखा जाता है — इसे **मात्रा** कहते हैं।

- क + **आ** = **का** (ा)
- क + **इ** = **कि** (ि)
- क + **ई** = **की** (ी)

**अ** की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती — वह हर व्यंजन में पहले से छिपा है।

steps.title: आ की मात्रा ( ा )
steps.body: व्यंजन के **बाद** खड़ी लकीर: **माला, राजा, नाना, आम, काला, दादा, बादल, ताला**।

steps.title: इ की मात्रा ( ि ) और ई की मात्रा ( ी )
आम गलती: छोटी इ और बड़ी ई
steps.body: **दिन** (day) और **दीन** (poor/humble) — अलग शब्द, अलग अर्थ! छोटी इ को छोटा बोलो, बड़ी ई को लंबा। और याद रखो: ि की लकीर अक्षर से **पहले** आती है, भले ही आवाज़ बाद में आए।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'क' के साथ तीनों मात्राएँ लगाओ: का, कि, की। अब 'म' के साथ: मा, मि, मी। 'नाना', 'नानी', 'नदी' लिखो।

activity.prompt: किस शब्द में कौन-सी मात्रा है? (Which matra?)

quiz.why: क के साथ ई की मात्रा 'ी' लगाने पर 'की' बनता है।

quiz.q: Which matra is written BEFORE the letter?
quiz.why: छोटी इ की मात्रा 'ि' अक्षर के पहले लिखी जाती है, जैसे 'कि'। बाकी मात्राएँ अक्षर के बाद या नीचे लगती हैं।
'नदी' का अर्थ river है, यानी बहता हुआ बड़ा पानी का रास्ता।

quiz.q: किस अक्षर की मात्रा नहीं होती?
quiz.why: 'अ' की कोई मात्रा नहीं होती, क्योंकि वह हर व्यंजन में पहले से छिपा होता है। आ, इ और ई की मात्राएँ होती हैं।
'राजा' में रा और जा में 'ा' की मात्रा है, जो आ की मात्रा है।

lessons.title: उ, ऊ, ऋ की मात्राएँ (u, oo, ri signs)

scenes.text: कोलकाता के फूल-बाज़ार में अर्जुन अपनी नानी के साथ जाता है।
दुकान पर लिखा है: **फूल**, **गुलाब**, **सूरजमुखी**।
नानी कहती हैं: 'नीचे लगने वाली मात्राएँ देखो — **ु** छोटा उ, **ू** बड़ा ऊ।'
घर लौटकर अर्जुन लिखता है: गुड़िया, भालू, कछुआ।

steps.title: उ की मात्रा ( ु )
steps.body: अक्षर के **नीचे** छोटा मोड़: **गुलाब, कुत्ता, गुड़िया, मुकुट, सुबह, चुप**।

steps.title: ऊ की मात्रा ( ू )
steps.body: अक्षर के नीचे उल्टा मोड़: **फूल, भालू, झूला, सूरज, दूध, आलू**।

steps.title: र के साथ ध्यान
steps.body: **र** के साथ ये मात्राएँ बगल में लगती हैं: **रु** (रुपया) और **रू** (रूमाल)। यह अलग दिखता है, इसलिए खास याद रखो।

steps.title: ऋ की मात्रा ( ृ )
steps.body: अक्षर के नीचे छोटा हुक: **कृपा, गृह, मृग, वृक्ष, कृषि**। (ऋ की आवाज़ हिंदी में अक्सर 'रि' जैसी बोली जाती है।)

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने घर की चार चीज़ें लिखो जिनमें उ या ऊ की मात्रा हो: झाड़ू, चूल्हा, कुर्सी, तराज़ू।

activity.prompt: सही मात्रा लगाकर शब्द पूरा करो (Write the full word).

quiz.why: 'फूल' में फ के साथ बड़े ऊ की मात्रा 'ू' है।
सही शब्द 'सूरज' है। बाकी शब्दों में गलत मात्रा या अक्षर हैं।
'वृक्ष' का अर्थ पेड़, यानी tree है।
र के साथ बड़े ऊ की मात्रा लगाने पर 'रू' बनता है, जैसे रूमाल में।
'कुत्ता' में कु पर छोटे उ की मात्रा 'ु' है।

lessons.title: ए, ऐ, ओ, औ, अं और ँ

scenes.text: इंदौर में दशहरे के **मेले** में तान्या और उसका दोस्त ओमर जाते हैं।
एक बोर्ड पर लिखा है: **मिठाइयाँ** — 'ऊपर का चाँद-बिंदु क्या है?' ओमर पूछता है।
तान्या: 'यह आवाज़ को नाक से बुलवाता है — **चंद्रबिंदु**!'

steps.title: ए ( े ) और ऐ ( ै )
steps.body:
- **े** — अक्षर के ऊपर एक तिरछी लकीर: **मेला, केला, सेब, पेड़, रेल**
- **ै** — दो तिरछी लकीरें: **पैसा, बैल, मैदान, थैला, कैसे**

steps.title: ओ ( ो ) और औ ( ौ )
steps.body:
- **ो** — आ की लकीर के ऊपर एक तिरछी लकीर: **मोर, घोड़ा, खिलौना, रोटी, सोना**
- **ौ** — लकीर के ऊपर दो तिरछी लकीरें: **कौआ, औरत, नौका, चौका, मौसम**

steps.title: अनुस्वार ( ं ) और चंद्रबिंदु ( ँ )
steps.body:
- **अनुस्वार ( ं )** — ऊपर एक बिंदु, 'न/म' जैसी आवाज़: **अंगूर, पतंग, गंगा, संतरा, कंघी**
- **चंद्रबिंदु ( ँ )** — चाँद और बिंदु, आवाज़ नाक से: **चाँद, माँ, आँख, हँसना, गाँव**

जब अक्षर के ऊपर पहले से कोई मात्रा हो (जैसे ि, े, ो), तो चंद्रबिंदु की जगह अक्सर सिर्फ़ बिंदु लिखते हैं: **मैं, हैं, नहीं**।

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body: **ए/ऐ** में उलझन: **बेल** (vine / a fruit) और **बैल** (ox) — अलग अर्थ! **ओ/औ**: **सोना** (gold / to sleep) और **सौ** (hundred)।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: 'क' पर हर मात्रा लगाकर पूरी बारहखड़ी लिखो: क का कि की कु कू के कै को कौ कं कः।

cards.back: क का कि की कु कू के कै को कौ कं कः

quiz.why: 'मोर' में म के साथ 'ो' की मात्रा है, जो ओ की मात्रा है।
'पैसा' में पै पर 'ै' की मात्रा है, जो ऐ की मात्रा है। सा में आ की मात्रा भी है।

quiz.q: 'चाँद' में ऊपर का चिह्न क्या कहलाता है?
quiz.why: 'चाँद' में ऊपर का चिह्न 'ँ' चंद्रबिंदु कहलाता है। अनुस्वार केवल बिंदु (ं) होता है।
'बैल' का अर्थ ox है, यानी खेत जोतने वाला जानवर।

quiz.q: बारहखड़ी में 'कु' के बाद क्या आता है?
quiz.why: बारहखड़ी में क, का, कि, की, कु, कू, के, कै, को, कौ क्रम से आते हैं। 'कु' के बाद 'कू' आता है।

scenes.text: मुंबई में दस साल का समीर अपनी दोस्त लीना को (जो अमेरिका में हिंदी सीख रही है) छोटे-छोटे वाक्यों में चिट्ठी लिखता है।
'आज रविवार है। मैं पार्क गया। वहाँ बहुत बच्चे थे।'
लीना जवाब देती है: 'मेरा नाम लीना है। मुझे आम पसंद है।'
दोनों ने छोटे वाक्यों से बड़ी दोस्ती कर ली!

steps.title: वाक्य क्या है?
steps.body:
शब्दों का ऐसा समूह जिससे **पूरी बात** समझ आए, **वाक्य** कहलाता है।

- **राम खाना खाता है।** ✅
- **खाना राम** ❌ (बात पूरी नहीं)

हिंदी में अक्सर क्रम होता है: **कौन + क्या/किसे + क्या करता है**: *सीता (कौन) किताब (क्या) पढ़ती है (क्या करती है)।*

steps.title: पूर्ण विराम और प्रश्नचिह्न
steps.body:
हिंदी में वाक्य के अंत में **पूर्ण विराम ( । )** लगता है — अंग्रेज़ी के full stop की तरह।

प्रश्न के अंत में **?** लगाओ: *तुम्हारा नाम क्या है?*

भाव दिखाने के लिए **!**: *वाह! कितना सुंदर!*

steps.title: आम गलती
steps.body:
- *मैं खुश है* ❌ → *मैं खुश **हूँ*** ✅
- *लड़के खेल रहा है* ❌ → *लड़के खेल **रहे हैं*** ✅
- वाक्य के अंत में । लगाना मत भूलो।

steps.title: करके देखो
steps.body: अपने बारे में पाँच वाक्य लिखो: मेरा नाम… है। मैं … कक्षा में पढ़ता/पढ़ती हूँ। मुझे … पसंद है।

activity.prompt: शब्दों को सही क्रम में लगाकर वाक्य बनाओ (Put the words in order).

quiz.why: 'मैं' के साथ 'हूँ' लगता है, इसलिए सही वाक्य 'मैं खुश हूँ।' है।

quiz.q: हिंदी में वाक्य के अंत में कौन-सा चिह्न लगता है?
quiz.why: हिंदी वाक्य के अंत में पूर्ण विराम (।) लगता है। अंग्रेज़ी में full stop (.) लगता है।
'बच्चे' एक से अधिक हैं, इसलिए 'खेल रहे हैं' लगेगा। 'हैं' बहुत के लिए आता है।
प्रश्नवाचक वाक्य कुछ पूछता है और अंत में ? लगता है। 'तुम कहाँ रहते हो?' एक प्रश्न है।
'मुझे आम पसंद है' का अर्थ है I like mangoes। 'पसंद' का मतलब like है।

questions.why: क के साथ 'ा' (आ की मात्रा) लगाने पर 'का' बनता है।
'माँ' में ऊपर चंद्रबिंदु (ँ) है। इससे आवाज़ नाक से निकलती है।
'दूध' में द पर बड़े ऊ की मात्रा 'ू' है।

questions.q: ि की मात्रा अक्षर के कहाँ लिखी जाती है?
questions.why: छोटी इ की मात्रा (ि) अक्षर के पहले लिखी जाती है, पर बोली बाद में जाती है। जैसे 'कि' में।
'केला' में के पर 'े' की मात्रा है, जो ए की मात्रा है।
सही शब्द 'कौआ' है, यानी crow। इसमें 'ौ' की मात्रा है।

questions.q: 'पतंग' में ऊपर का बिंदु कहलाता है…
questions.why: 'पतंग' में ऊपर का बिंदु (ं) अनुस्वार कहलाता है।

questions.q: 'दिन' और 'दीन' में अंतर किस मात्रा का है?
questions.why: 'दिन' में छोटी इ की मात्रा है और 'दीन' में बड़ी ई की मात्रा है। यही अंतर है।
'लड़कियाँ' बहुत हैं, इसलिए 'गा रही हैं' लगेगा। स्त्रीलिंग और बहुवचन दोनों मिलते हैं।
र के साथ छोटे उ की मात्रा 'ु' लगाने पर 'रु' बनता है, जैसे रुपया में।
'वृक्ष' में व पर 'ृ' की मात्रा है, जो ऋ की मात्रा है।

questions.q: बारहखड़ी में 'को' के बाद क्या आता है?
questions.why: बारहखड़ी में क्रम है: के, कै, को, कौ, कं, कः। 'को' के बाद 'कौ' आता है।

courses.title: हिंदी कक्षा 4–5: व्याकरण, शब्द-भंडार और लेखन (Grammar, vocabulary & writing)
courses.summary: Learn संज्ञा, सर्वनाम, विशेषण and क्रिया, change लिंग and वचन, build vocabulary with पर्यायवाची and विलोम, and write a short अनुच्छेद and a letter — with an original poem to enjoy.

Learners can use common synonyms (पर्यायवाची) and opposites (विलोम)
