- *'Sorry, but you started it.'*
- *'Sorry if you feel bad.'*
- A laughing 'sorry'.

These don't take responsibility. A real apology has **no 'but'**.

steps.title: Forgiving
steps.body: When someone truly says sorry, try to forgive. Forgiving doesn't mean what happened was OK — it means you're ready to move on. If someone keeps hurting you again and again, tell a trusted adult.

steps.title: It takes courage
steps.body: Saying sorry is brave. It shows you are strong enough to admit a mistake.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Think of a time you hurt someone (even by accident). Practise a 4-part apology in your head.

activity.prompt: Put the parts of a real apology in order.
items: Say it was wrong and how it hurt

options: 'I'm sorry I pushed you. It was wrong. I'll be careful next time.'
quiz.why: A real apology says what you did was wrong and promises to do better. 'I'm sorry I pushed you. It was wrong. I'll be careful next time.' does this.
Saying sorry is brave, because it takes courage to admit a mistake. It is not weak.

options: You are ready to move on
quiz.why: Forgiving means you are ready to move on. It does not mean what happened was fine, or that you must be best friends.

quiz.q: If someone hurts you again and again, you should…
quiz.why: If someone keeps hurting you, tell a trusted adult. Hurting back or staying quiet will not stop it.
A real apology has no 'but', because 'but' cancels the apology by blaming someone else.

questions.q: Which is a magic word for asking?
questions.why: 'Please' is a magic word for asking nicely.
Telling the truth builds trust, because people know they can believe you.

questions.q: Which feeling might someone sitting alone have?
questions.why: Someone sitting alone may feel lonely or sad. It is good to notice and be kind.

questions.q: You get extra change by mistake. You…
questions.why: If you get extra change by mistake, return it. This is being honest.
Everyone deserves good manners, whether they are adults, children, friends or strangers.

questions.q: A good way to calm anger is…
questions.why: Slow breathing helps calm anger. Shouting, hitting or running into the road is harmful.

options: 'I'm sorry I took your pen. I'll give it back and ask first next time.'
questions.why: The best apology says what you did, says sorry, offers to fix it, and promises to do better. 'Sorry, but…' and 'Sorry if…' are not real apologies.

options: Saying something true in a gentle way
questions.why: Being honest and kind means saying something true in a gentle way. Mean truths hurt and lies are not honest.

options: Notice a friend is upset and ask if they're OK
questions.why: Empathy is shown when you notice that a friend is upset and ask if they are OK. Ignoring or laughing is the opposite.

questions.q: Why do lies often make people worried?
options: They have to remember and hide the lie
questions.why: People who lie have to remember the lie and hide the truth, which makes them worried.

questions.q: A new child from another country greets you differently. Good manners mean…
options: Respecting it and sharing how you greet
questions.why: Good manners mean respecting a different way of greeting and sharing your own. Ignoring, laughing or saying it is wrong is rude.

questions.q: Your friend says sorry but keeps doing the same hurtful thing every day. What should you do?
questions.why: If a friend says sorry but keeps hurting you every day, tell a trusted adult. Repeated hurt needs adult help.

courses.title: Good friends and standing up to bullying
courses.summary: Learn what makes a healthy friendship, how to sort out disagreements, what bullying is (and isn't), and what to do if you are bullied, see bullying, or have been unkind yourself.
outcomes: Learners can describe qualities of a good friend and solve small disagreements fairly
Learners can tell the difference between a one-time conflict and bullying
Learners can use safe responses and know whom to tell if they are bullied
Learners can act as a helpful bystander
Learners who have bullied can understand the harm, apologise and change
courses.guardianNote: Covers healthy friendship, conflict resolution, and bullying (physical, verbal, social and cyber) for ages 8–11: how to respond, how to be a helpful bystander, and how children who have bullied can change. Non-graphic, age-appropriate, and focused on telling trusted adults; lists Childline 1098 and emergency 112. Please talk through the scenarios with your child and let them know they can always come to you.

scenes.text: In Chennai, Arjun has two friends. Vikram always wants to choose the game and laughs when Arjun misses a goal.
Daniel, who moved from Singapore, takes turns choosing, passes the ball, and says 'Nice try!'
Arjun notices he feels small around Vikram and happy around Daniel.
He tells Vikram calmly: 'I want to choose sometimes too.' Vikram thinks about it and agrees. Friendships can grow.

steps.title: Signs of a good friendship
steps.body:
A good friend:

- is kind and honest with you
- takes turns and shares
- listens when you talk
- says sorry when they're wrong
- is happy when you do well
- respects your 'no'
- doesn't make you do things that feel wrong or unsafe

steps.title: Disagreements are normal
steps.body:
Friends sometimes disagree. Solve it like this:

1. **Cool down** first.
2. Each person says **what they want and feel** using 'I' words: *'I feel left out when…'*
3. **Listen** without interrupting.
4. Find a **fair solution**: take turns, mix both ideas, or toss a coin.
5. Shake hands or smile and move on.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.body: If a 'friend' often makes fun of you, leaves you out on purpose, threatens 'I won't be your friend if you don't…', or makes you feel bad most of the time, that's not a healthy friendship. It's OK to spend time with other people.

steps.title: Making new friends
steps.body: Smile, say hello, ask questions (*'What games do you like?'*), invite someone to join you, and be patient — friendships take time.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write the names of two people you trust. What do they do that makes you feel safe and happy?

activity.prompt: Am I being a good friend? Tick the ones you did this week.
items: I took turns choosing a game
I listened when a friend was talking
I said something kind or encouraging
I said sorry when I was wrong
I included someone who was alone
I kept a friend's (safe) secret or surprise
I respected when a friend said no

quiz.q: Which is a sign of a good friend?
quiz.why: A good friend takes turns and listens. Leaving you out, threatening you or laughing at your mistakes is not friendly.

quiz.q: 'I won't be your friend if you don't give me your lunch.' This is…
quiz.why: 'I won't be your friend if you don't give me your lunch' is pressure and a threat, which is a warning sign, not real friendship.

quiz.q: The first step in solving a disagreement is…
quiz.why: The first step in solving a disagreement is cooling down. It is easier to talk when you are calm.

options: 'I feel left out when I'm not picked.'
quiz.why: 'I' statements describe your own feeling without blaming, like 'I feel left out when I'm not picked.'

quiz.q: Is it normal for friends to disagree sometimes?
quiz.why: Yes, friends can disagree sometimes. It is normal, and we can solve it fairly.

scenes.text: In a school in Delhi, Class 4 discusses three stories.
Story 1: Rahul and Aman argue once about who won a race, then make up. — **Conflict**, not bullying.
Story 2: Every day, a group calls Priya names about her skin colour and hides her bag. — **Bullying**.
Story 3: Someone posts a mean edited photo of Joe in a class chat, and others keep sharing it. — **Cyberbullying**.

steps.title: Bullying: three signs
steps.body:
**Bullying** is when someone:

1. **hurts** another person on purpose (body, words, or feelings),
2. **again and again** (repeated), and
3. has **more power** (older, bigger, more popular, or in a group).

A single fight between equals is a **conflict** — still not OK to hurt, but different.

steps.title: Types of bullying
steps.body:
- **Physical**: hitting, pushing, kicking, taking or breaking things.
- **Verbal**: name-calling, insults, mean jokes about looks, skin colour, caste, religion, disability, accent, gender, family.
- **Social**: leaving out on purpose, spreading rumours, making others stop being friends.
- **Cyber**: mean messages, posting embarrassing photos, fake accounts, group-chat exclusion.

steps.title: It's never the bullied child's fault
steps.body: Nobody deserves to be bullied — not because of how they look, talk, dress, learn, or where they come from. Bullying says something about the person doing it, not about you.

steps.title: It's not 'just teasing'
steps.body: If the other person isn't laughing too, or it keeps happening, it's not a joke. Adults should take it seriously.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Sort the situations below into 'conflict' and 'bullying'.

activity.prompt: Is it a one-time conflict or bullying?

items.text: Two friends argue once over a game, then make up
A group calls a girl names every day
Someone keeps sharing a mean photo of a classmate
Two classmates disagree on a project idea
An older boy takes a younger boy's lunch money every week
Kids leave one child out of every game on purpose, every day

quiz.q: Which three things usually make something bullying?
quiz.why: Bullying is usually on purpose, repeated, and there is an imbalance of power. One accident or a fight between equals is different.
Spreading rumours hurts someone's friendships and reputation, so it is social bullying.
Bullying is never the fault of the child being bullied. The person who bullies is responsible for what they do.

quiz.q: Mean messages in a group chat are…
quiz.why: Mean messages in a group chat are cyberbullying, which is bullying done online.

quiz.q: 'It was just a joke' — but the other child is crying and it happens daily. This is…
quiz.why: If the other child is crying and it happens every day, it is not just a joke. It is bullying.

lessons.title: If you are bullied, or you see bullying

scenes.text: In Pune, every day at the bus stop, an older boy, Nitin, snatches 9-year-old Sam's cap and laughs.
Sam feels sick every morning and doesn't want to go to school.
His classmate Aditi sees it. She stands next to Sam and says, 'Come on, Sam, let's wait over here.' Then she tells the bus attendant.
Sam tells his mother and class teacher. The school talks to Nitin and his parents. The snatching stops.

steps.title: If you are being bullied
steps.body:
- **Stay calm** on the outside: stand tall, look at them, say firmly *'Stop. I don't like that.'* and walk away towards adults or friends.
- **Don't fight back** — you could get hurt or in trouble.
- **Stay near** friends and adults.
- **Tell** a trusted adult — parent, teacher, counsellor. Keep telling until someone helps.
- **Write down** what happened, when and who saw it.

steps.title: If you see bullying (bystander)
steps.body:
Bystanders have great power — bullying often stops when others don't laugh or join in.

- **Don't laugh** or share.
- **Be with** the person: *'Come sit with us.'*
- **Speak up** if it's safe: *'That's not cool. Stop.'*
- **Tell an adult** — that's **reporting**, not tattling. Tattling is to get someone in trouble; reporting is to get someone **out of** trouble.

steps.title: Where to get help in India
steps.body:
- Trusted adults at home and school; your school counsellor.
- **1098** — Childline, free, 24 hours, for children who need help.
- **112** — any emergency where someone is in danger.

steps.title: When it's serious
steps.body: If you're hurt, threatened, or someone tries to make you do something unsafe, get away and tell an adult **immediately**. If feelings of sadness or fear don't go away, talking to a counsellor helps.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise saying 'Stop. I don't like that.' in a strong, calm voice in front of a mirror.

a.text: At recess, two classmates keep calling Meena 'fatty' and laughing. Others are watching. You're nearby. What do you do?

choices.label: Laugh along so they don't pick on you
choices.feedback: Laughing makes the bullies feel powerful and hurts Meena more.

choices.label: Walk over and say to Meena, 'Come play with us.'
choices.feedback: Being with her takes away the audience and shows she's not alone.

choices.label: Do nothing and look away
choices.feedback: Doing nothing can feel safer, but Meena still feels alone.

b.text: Meena runs off crying. How could you help now?

choices.label: Find Meena and say 'That wasn't OK. Are you alright?'
choices.feedback: It's never too late to be kind.

b2.text: You feel bad watching. What's a safe thing you can still do?

choices.label: Tell a teacher what you saw
choices.feedback: Reporting helps someone get out of trouble.

choices.label: Join Meena and invite her to play
choices.feedback: Great choice.

c.text: Meena comes with you. The name-callers look surprised. Should an adult know?

choices.label: Yes — tell the teacher after recess
choices.feedback: Right. It has been happening; adults need to know.

choices.label: No — it's tattling
choices.feedback: Telling to protect someone is reporting, not tattling.

e.text: Reporting keeps people safe. Want to tell the teacher?

choices.label: Yes, I'll tell the teacher
choices.feedback: Good.

d.text: The teacher thanks you and talks with everyone involved. Meena says, 'Thanks for standing with me.' You were an upstander!

quiz.q: If someone bullies you, a good first response is…
options: Say 'Stop, I don't like that' firmly and walk to a safe adult
quiz.why: If someone bullies you, firmly say 'Stop, I don't like that', then walk to a safe adult. Hitting back or giving in does not help.

quiz.q: Telling a teacher about bullying is…
quiz.why: Telling a teacher about bullying is reporting, to keep someone safe. It is not mean.
Childline's number in India is 1098. It is free and open 24 hours.

options: Stand with the bullied child and tell an adult
quiz.why: A bystander can stand with the bullied child and tell an adult. Joining in, laughing or sharing a video makes it worse.

quiz.q: What if the first adult you tell doesn't help?
quiz.why: If the first adult doesn't help, tell another trusted adult. Keep telling until someone helps.

lessons.title: If I have been unkind: changing course

scenes.text: After the school meeting, Nitin (from the last lesson) sits with the counsellor, Ms Thomas.
'I just thought it was funny. My older cousins do it to me,' he says quietly.
Ms Thomas listens. 'It sounds like you know how it feels. How do you think Sam felt?'
Nitin apologises to Sam, returns his cap, and joins the school's buddy programme for younger kids. He feels better about himself.

steps.title: Anyone can change
steps.body: People who bully are not 'bad forever'. Sometimes they are being hurt themselves, want to feel powerful or popular, or don't realise how much it hurts. Bullying is a **behaviour** — and behaviours can change.

steps.title: Steps to change
steps.body:
1. **Notice**: *'Was what I did hurtful? Did it happen more than once?'*
2. **Imagine**: *'How would I feel if someone did this to me?'*
3. **Stop** — even if friends want you to continue.
4. **Apologise** sincerely (4-part apology) and repair: return things, delete posts.
5. **Talk** to a trusted adult about what's going on for you.

steps.title: Feeling strong in good ways
steps.body: Real strength is helping: being a buddy to younger kids, being great at a sport or art, making people laugh **with** you, not **at** others.

steps.title: If someone is hurting you at home or elsewhere
steps.body: If you are being hurt by someone, it's not your fault. Tell a trusted adult or call **1098**.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Write privately below. No one else will see it.

activity.prompt: Think of a time you were unkind to someone (even small). How might they have felt, and what could you do now to make it right?
activity.hint: Be honest with yourself. Write one action you can take this week.

quiz.why: Bullying is a behaviour, and behaviour can change. People can learn to be kind.

quiz.q: If friends want you to keep teasing someone, you…
quiz.why: If friends want you to keep teasing, stop even if they don't. Choosing kindness is brave.

quiz.q: A way to repair after cyberbullying is…
quiz.why: After cyberbullying, deleting the posts and apologising helps repair the harm. Posting more or making a fake account makes it worse.
Real strength is helping others and being kind. Scaring or laughing at people is not strength.

quiz.q: Imagining how the other person felt is called…
quiz.why: Imagining how the other person felt is called empathy.

questions.why: A good friend takes turns. Leaving you out, threatening you or laughing at you is not friendly.
Childline in India is 1098, a free helpline for children.
Name-calling that is repeated and on purpose is bullying. It is verbal bullying.

questions.q: Hiding someone's bag every day is…
questions.why: Hiding someone's bag every day causes repeated harm, so it is bullying, physical or social.

questions.q: A bystander who helps is called an…
questions.why: A bystander who helps the bullied child is called an upstander.

questions.q: Telling an adult to keep someone safe is…
questions.why: Telling an adult to keep someone safe is reporting. Tattling is telling just to get someone in trouble.

questions.q: Two equals argue once and make up. This is…
questions.why: A single argument between equals who make up is a conflict, not bullying, because bullying is repeated and has unequal power.

questions.q: If you're bullied, why shouldn't you fight back?
options: You could get hurt or in trouble
questions.why: Fighting back can get you hurt or into trouble. It is safer to get help from an adult.

options: 'I feel upset when the rules change mid-game.'
questions.why: An 'I' statement says how you feel without attacking. 'I feel upset when the rules change mid-game' does this.

questions.q: A classmate is left out of the group chat on purpose and mocked there. This is…
questions.why: Leaving a classmate out of a group chat on purpose and mocking them there is cyberbullying.

questions.q: Someone who bullied others realises it was wrong. Best next step?
options: Stop, apologise, repair, and talk to an adult
questions.why: If you realise you bullied someone, stop, apologise, repair the harm and talk to an adult. Hiding or blaming others does not help.

questions.q: A child is bullied because of their caste or religion. What is true?
options: It is never their fault and adults must act
questions.why: Bullying someone for their caste or religion is never their fault. No one deserves it, and adults must act.

courses.title: Safe online, safe me: privacy and online safety basics
courses.summary: Learn what personal information is and why to keep it private, how to spot tricks and strangers online, how to be kind and balanced with screens, and the basics of body privacy, safe secrets and saying no.
outcomes: Learners can identify personal information and keep it private online
Learners can recognise online tricks (scams, fake prizes, strangers asking for photos or secrets) and respond safely
Learners can use strong passwords and ask before downloading or buying
Learners can describe healthy screen habits and kind online behaviour
Learners can explain body privacy, safe vs unsafe secrets, and how to tell a trusted adult
courses.guardianNote: Covers online privacy, scams and grooming red flags, kind online behaviour and screen balance, plus body-privacy basics (private parts, safe/unsafe touch, surprises vs unsafe secrets, saying no, telling trusted adults) for ages 8–11, following UNESCO ITGSE 2018 age-appropriate key ideas. Non-explicit and reassuring: it repeatedly states it is never the child's fault and that telling is always right. Lists Childline 1098, cybercrime helpline 1930 and emergency 112. Please go through the 'safety hand' activity with your child.

story.title: The quiz that wanted too much

scenes.text: In Bengaluru, 9-year-old Ishaan plays a game on his mother's phone. A pop-up says: 'Find out your superhero name! Enter your full name, school and address.'
He starts typing, then stops. 'Why would a superhero game need my address?'
He shows his mother. She says, 'Great thinking! That's private information. Strangers could misuse it.'
They close the pop-up together.

steps.title: What is personal (private) information?
steps.body:
Information that tells someone **who you are or where to find you**:

- full name, home address, school name
- phone number, email
- passwords and PINs
- date of birth
- photos in school uniform or showing your house number
- where you'll be and when ('at the park at 5')

steps.title: Safe to share vs keep private
steps.body:
Usually **OK** (with friends you know): your favourite colour, food, cartoon, a nickname.
**Keep private** online: anything from the list above. **Ask a parent** before sharing photos or videos.

steps.title: Strong passwords
steps.body:
- Use long passphrases: *PurpleMango!Runs7Fast*.
- Never share passwords with friends — only with parents.
- Don't use your name or birthday.
- Log out on shared devices.

steps.title: Ask first
steps.body: Always ask a parent before downloading apps, clicking links, entering details, or buying anything — even 'free' games can ask for payments.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: With a parent, check the privacy settings on one app or game you use.

activity.prompt: Is it OK to share online, or keep private?

items.text: A photo showing your house number

quiz.why: A home address is private, because it shows where you live. Favourite song, food and colour are safe to share.
Only your parents or guardians should know your password. Do not share it with friends or anyone online.

quiz.q: A game asks for your school name and address. You…
quiz.why: If a game asks for your school name and address, stop and ask a parent. Do not type it.
A strong password is long and mixed, like 'PurpleMango!Runs7Fast'. 'password', '1234' and 'rahul' are easy to guess.

quiz.q: Before downloading an app, you should…
quiz.why: Before downloading an app, ask a parent. Some apps are not safe.

scenes.text: In Lucknow, Zoya, 10, plays an online game. A player named 'CoolGamer99' messages her: 'Hi! I'm 11 too. Want 1000 free coins? Just send me your password.'
Later: 'Let's keep our chats secret. Send me a photo of you?'
Zoya feels uncomfortable. She remembers: secrets + photos + 'free' = red flags.
She doesn't reply, takes a screenshot, and tells her father. They block and report the account in the game.

steps.title: People online may not be who they say
steps.body: Anyone can pretend to be a child online. A '10-year-old girl' could be an adult. Never trust someone just because they seem friendly or say they're your age.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body:
Tell a trusted adult right away if someone online:

- asks for **photos** of you, or sends you pictures that make you uncomfortable
- asks you to **keep secrets** from parents
- offers **gifts, free coins, prizes**
- asks for **passwords, addresses or phone numbers**
- wants to **video chat** or **meet in person**
- makes you feel **scared, confused or worried**

steps.title: Stop – Block – Screenshot – Tell
steps.body:
1. **Stop**: don't reply.
2. **Block** and **report** the account.
3. **Screenshot** the messages (to show an adult).
4. **Tell** a trusted adult.

You will **not** be in trouble for telling — it's always the right choice.

steps.title: Help in India
steps.body: Childline **1098** (free, 24 hours). For online crimes, adults can call the cybercrime helpline **1930** or report at the national cybercrime reporting portal. In danger: **112**.

steps.title: Scams
steps.body: 'You've won a new phone!', 'Click to claim your prize!', 'Your account will be deleted unless…' — these are tricks to steal information or money. Don't click. Show an adult.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Make a family rule card: 'If anything online feels weird, I'll show Mum/Dad, and I won't be in trouble.'

a.text: A player you don't know in real life messages: 'You're so good at this game! Let's be best friends. What school do you go to?'

choices.label: Tell them your school
choices.feedback: Your school name helps a stranger find you in real life.

choices.label: Don't share — reply 'I don't share personal info' or don't reply
choices.feedback: Good: you kept private info private.

b.text: They now ask, 'Send me a photo in your uniform. Keep this our secret!'

choices.label: Send it — they seem nice
choices.feedback: Asking for photos and secrets are big red flags.

choices.label: Stop, screenshot and tell a parent
choices.feedback: Yes — telling is always right, even if you shared something before.

d.text: This is a dangerous situation. What's the right move now?

choices.label: Stop replying and tell a trusted adult immediately
choices.feedback: You did the right thing by telling. It's not your fault.

c.text: They reply: 'OK! Want 5000 free gems? Just send your password.'

choices.label: Send the password
choices.feedback: No real friend or game needs your password.

choices.label: Block, report and tell a parent
choices.feedback: Perfect: Stop, Block, Screenshot, Tell.

e.text: Your parent thanks you, helps you block and report the account. You stayed safe — and you're not in trouble. Telling is brave.

quiz.q: Someone online asks you to keep your chats secret from parents. This is…
options: A red flag — tell an adult
quiz.why: If someone online asks you to keep chats secret from your parents, it is a red flag. Tell an adult.

quiz.q: What does 'Stop, Block, Screenshot, Tell' mean?
options: Steps to stay safe from bad messages
quiz.why: 'Stop, Block, Screenshot, Tell' is a set of steps to stay safe from bad messages.

quiz.q: A message says 'You won a free phone! Click here.' You…
options: Don't click and show an adult
quiz.why: A message that says you won a free phone is likely a scam. Don't click, and show it to an adult.

quiz.q: Can people pretend to be children online?
quiz.why: Yes, anyone can pretend to be a child online, so you cannot be sure who someone really is.

quiz.q: If you already shared something you shouldn't have, you should…
options: Tell a trusted adult — you won't be in trouble
Delete your account and say nothing
quiz.why: If you already shared something you shouldn't have, tell a trusted adult. You won't be in trouble, and they can help.

scenes.text: In Kochi, Class 5 has a group chat for homework. Someone posts a funny but mean meme about a classmate, Rinku.
Lots of children react with 😂. Anjali almost does too.
She thinks: 'Would I say this to Rinku's face? Would I like it about me?' She doesn't react, and messages: 'Let's keep this group for homework.'
That night, Anjali also notices she's been on the tablet for 3 hours and her eyes hurt. She goes to read instead.

steps.title: Think before you post: T.H.I.N.K.
steps.body:
Is it **T**rue? **H**elpful? **I**nspiring? **N**ecessary? **K**ind?

If not, don't post it. Remember: things online can be copied and shared forever, even if you delete them.

steps.title: Don't join in
steps.body: Reacting with 😂 to a mean post or forwarding it is joining in. Instead: don't react, support the person privately, and tell an adult if it continues.

steps.title: Healthy screen habits
steps.body:
- Put screens away at least an hour before bed (screens can make it harder to fall asleep).
- No screens at meals — talk instead.
- Take breaks: every 20 minutes, look at something far away for 20 seconds.
- Balance with outdoor play, reading, hobbies and family time.
- Agree on screen rules with your family.

steps.title: Not everything online is true
steps.body: Videos and photos can be edited or made by computers. Check with an adult or a trusted source before believing or sharing surprising news.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Use the slider to think about your screen time for fun on a school day.

activity.label: How many hours of fun screen time (games, videos) do you have on a school day?

bands.text: A balanced amount for many children — leaves time for play, homework, reading and sleep.
OK for many families if it doesn't cut into sleep, homework, outdoor play or meals. Talk with your family about your rules.
That's a lot. Notice: do you feel tired, grumpy or have sore eyes? Try swapping some time for outdoor play or a hobby.
Very high. It can affect sleep, mood, eyes and schoolwork. Make a plan with a parent to cut down step by step.

quiz.why: In T.H.I.N.K., the K stands for Kind. Before posting, ask if it is True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary and Kind.

quiz.q: Reacting 😂 to a mean meme about a classmate is…
quiz.why: Reacting with a laugh to a mean meme about a classmate encourages it, so you are joining in the unkindness.

quiz.q: Why put screens away before bed?
options: They can make it harder to sleep
quiz.why: Put screens away before bed, because they can make it harder to sleep, and sleep is important.

quiz.q: Can a deleted post still be shared?
options: Yes, others may have copied it
quiz.why: Yes, a deleted post can still be shared, because others may have copied it or taken a screenshot.

quiz.q: The 20-20-20 idea: every 20 minutes look at something far away for…
quiz.why: In the 20-20-20 idea, every 20 minutes look at something far away for 20 seconds, to rest your eyes.

lessons.title: My body is mine: privacy, safe secrets and saying no

scenes.text: In Jaipur, Tara's aunt says, 'Let's keep Mummy's birthday cake a surprise until Sunday!' Tara giggles and agrees.
Later, an older cousin says, 'Don't tell anyone I hit you, or you'll be in trouble.' Tara feels a heavy, bad feeling.
She remembers her school lesson: **surprises** are happy and end soon; **unsafe secrets** feel bad and should be told.
Tara tells her mother. Her mother says, 'Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing. It's not your fault.'

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body: Your body belongs to **you**. Private parts are the parts covered by underwear/swimsuit. Nobody should touch them, look at them or ask you to show them — and nobody should ask you to touch theirs — except to keep you clean and healthy (for example, a parent helping a young child, or a doctor checking you **with a parent present**).

steps.title: Safe and unsafe touch
steps.body:
- **Safe touch** feels OK: a high-five, a hug you want from family, a doctor's check with a parent there.
- **Unsafe touch** hurts, scares you, or touches private parts, or comes with 'don't tell'.
- You can say **NO** to any touch, even a hug, even from someone you know: *'No, I don't want a hug. High-five?'*

steps.title: Surprises vs secrets
steps.body:
- **Surprise**: happy, everyone finds out soon (a gift, a party).
- **Unsafe secret**: makes you feel worried, scared or confused, and someone says 'never tell'.

**Always tell** unsafe secrets to a trusted adult. Keeping you safe is more important than any promise.

steps.title: My safety hand
steps.body: Trace your hand and write on each finger the name of a trusted adult you could tell (parent, grandparent, teacher, school counsellor, aunt). If one doesn't listen, tell the next. You can also call **1098** (Childline).

steps.title: It's never your fault
steps.body: If anyone ever touches you in an unsafe way, it is **never** your fault — even if it's someone you know, even if you didn't say no, even if they say you'll be in trouble. Tell. Adults will help.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Practise saying 'No! Stop! I'm going to tell.' in a strong voice with a parent.

activity.prompt: Questions children often wonder about but don't ask

items.q: What if the person is someone I know or love?
items.a: Rules about your body apply to everyone — family, friends, neighbours, teachers. If something feels wrong, tell another trusted adult.

items.q: What if I promised not to tell?
items.a: Promises to keep unsafe secrets don't count. Telling to stay safe is always OK.

items.q: Will I get in trouble for telling?
items.a: No. You did the right thing. A good adult will thank you and help.

items.q: Can I say no to a hug from a relative?
items.a: Yes. You can offer a wave, a namaste or a high-five instead. Your body, your choice.

items.q: What if the first adult doesn't believe me?
items.a: Keep telling other trusted adults until someone helps, or call 1098.

quiz.why: Your body belongs to you. You decide who touches it.

quiz.q: Which is a surprise (OK to keep for now)?
options: A stranger's message asking for photos
quiz.why: A birthday gift plan is a surprise: it is happy and ends soon, so it is OK to keep for now. The other examples are unsafe secrets.

quiz.q: Someone says 'Don't tell anyone, or you'll be in trouble.' You should…
quiz.why: If someone says 'Don't tell anyone, or you'll be in trouble', that is an unsafe secret. Tell a trusted adult.

quiz.q: Can you say no to a hug?
quiz.why: Yes, you can say no to a hug. You can choose another greeting like a wave or a high five.

quiz.q: If something unsafe happens, whose fault is it?
quiz.why: If something unsafe happens, it is never the child's fault. Tell a trusted adult.

questions.why: A password is private. Keep it secret from everyone except your parents. Favourite game, fruit and colour are safe.

questions.q: If something online feels weird, you should…
questions.why: If something online feels weird, tell a trusted adult. Hiding it or replying angrily does not keep you safe.
A surprise is happy and ends soon, like a party plan. It is different from an unsafe secret.
A long passphrase like 'MyDogEats3BlueMangoes!' is strong. Short or simple ones like '12345' or 'abcd' are easy to guess.

questions.q: Someone online offers free coins for your password. This is…
questions.why: Free coins in return for your password is a trick or scam. Never share passwords.
The Childline number in India is 1098, for children who need help.

questions.q: Before posting, ask if it's True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary and…
questions.why: In T.H.I.N.K., the K stands for Kind: ask if it is True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary and Kind.

questions.q: Who can you say 'no' to about touch?
questions.why: You can say no to touch from anyone, including people you know. Your body is yours.

questions.q: A player says they're 10, but asks for photos and secrecy. You should…
questions.why: A player who asks for photos and secrecy shows red flags. Stop, block, take a screenshot and tell an adult.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you post a photo in school uniform with your school name visible?
questions.why: A photo in uniform with the school name visible tells strangers where to find you.

questions.q: The first trusted adult doesn't listen. You…
options: Tell another trusted adult or call 1098
questions.why: If the first trusted adult doesn't listen, tell another trusted adult or call 1098. Keep telling until someone helps.

questions.q: Which situation needs telling an adult right away?
options: An adult asks you to keep a secret about touching
questions.why: If an adult asks you to keep a secret about touching, tell a trusted adult right away. It is an unsafe secret.
